speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have the honour to
inform the House that I have directed the
Clerk of the House to lay upon the table of the House my recommendation and his report in the matter of the proposed appointment of ten permanent translators on the staff of the House.
Mr. GEO. H. BRADBURY (Selkirk), moved that the third report of the Select Standing Committee on the Pollution of. Navigable Waters be concurred in.
What is nr that report?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The report recommends that the committee be appointed next year, and further;
That the Government endeavour to arrange during the coming recess of parliament for a conference of representatives of the Dominion of each of the provinces, of the International Waterways Commission, and the chairman of this committee, for the purpose of fully discussing the whole subject, with a view of endeavouring to overcome local difficulties, and of agreeing upon some form of remedial legislation -which could toe passed concurrently by the Dominion Parliament, and toy the legislatures of the various provinces.

The recommendation of the committee, that the Government should enter into a conference with the /various provinces, is certainly a good one, but the other recommendation, that the committee should be reappointed, is simply a pious wish which cannot have any binding force.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It would not bind Parliament next session.

This committee was appointed rather late in the session, and we did not have the opportunity that /we thought necessary to enable us to bring in a final report, but the witnesses that we have examined have given evidence which, I think, points to the absolute necessity of some federal legislation being enacted to prevent the pollution of our streams. The men examined, who were as well qualified as any men in Canada to express an opinion, have all agreed that the present conditions in Canada regarding the pollution of our great lakes and navigable streams are becoming alarming. While the report of the committee aEks for the continuance of the committee next year, the intention was simply to draw the attention of the House to the necessity of continuing this investigation next year. It does not mean that the present committee should be continued; at least, that was not the intention. It simply suggests that a committee with like powers he appointed next year. It is only a suggestion to the House. We thought it advisable that the different provinces should be asked to co-opef-

ate, and the report recommends that the Government request them to name representa-' tives to meet in conference during the recess to discuss what might best be done to arrive at some definite arrangement, as to the legislation which should be brought down. The object of the committee ;was, I think, to gather as far as possible an expression of opinion from the provinces as to how far they are willing /to go in this matter.

The idea presented in this report seems to me to be worthy of consideration, but the report appears to be open to two objections. First, as I have pointed out, the reappointment of the committee for next year would be out of order. The powers of this committee cease with the present session. Moreover, whilst for my part, I would altogether approve of the recommendation to the Government that during the recess they should organize a conference between representatives of the Dominion and of the provinces for the purpose of discussing the matter investigated by the committee, there is another recommendation which seems to be absolutely out of order also. Let me read it:
In conclusion your comittee, having in view the gravity of the present situation, and the importance of having 6ome action taken at as early a date as possible to prevent the continuance of the practice now so prevalent of
Diluting the waters of the country by the
ischarge thereinto of untreated sewage and other offensive matter, recommend that the Government endeavour to arrange, during the coming recess of Parliament, for a conference of representatives of the Dominion, of each of the provinces, of the International Waterways Commission, and the chairman of this committee.
The Chairman of this committee has no existence the moment we reach prorogation. If the Government choose to invite Mr. Bradbury to take part in the conference, I have no objection.
That was suggested by the committee; it was not my desire.

Perhaps my
hon. friend had better take back the report, and have it recast.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think it would be better to allow the report to stand, and if the right hon. gentleman desires to have it referred back to the committee, I have no objection. I think there are some objections to it in its present form.
Report stands.

Before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to ask the Minister of Labour if the time has not gone by when the United Shoe Machinery Com-Mr. BRADBURY.
pany should bring themselves within the order of the board regarding combination in restraint of trade. I understood that they had six months in which to do certain things, and that that period expired some time in the early part of May, and nothing has been done. Will the minister tell the House how the matter stands?

My hon. friend is quite right in saying that the six months allowed by the board expired early in May-on the 6th of May, I think. Nothing has been done since; we have been too busy with other matters; but I understand they have made certain alterations in their leases to meet the requirements of the report of the board. I have not examined into that, but that is the information I have received from their solicitor.

This morning's Ottawa Citizen publishes a despatch stating that the internal storage elevators are to be located, the one for Saskatchewan at Moose jaw, and the one for Alberta at Calgary. I ask the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce if that is correct.

A few days ago the Board of Grain Commissioners reported, recommending that an internal storage elevator should be built at Moosejaw and another at Saskatoon, in Saskatchewan. No recommendation has yet been made with regard to the location of the elevator in Alberta. Steps will he taken at once to follow the recommendation of the commissioners, and plans will be immediately prepared for the building of the elevators at Moosejaw and Saskatoon.

On motion of Hon. Frank Cochrane (Minister of Railways and Canals), House went into committee to consider certain proposed resolutions respecting the granting of the subsidies therein mentioned to certain railways companies. (See Debates, p. 11322.
(Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)
To the Margaree Coal and Railway Company, Limited, for the following lines of rail-
W^a) from a point on the Intercolonial railway near Orangedale to St. Rose; not exceeding 46 miles.	.
(b) from a point on the Intercolonial railway near McIntyre Lake to Caribou Cove, Port Malcolm, Richmond county; not exceeding 4 miles.
the said subsidies being granted m lieu ol subsidy granted by chapter 51 of 1910, section 1, item 4; not exceeding 50 miles.

Has any
work been done on this railway?

No. They inform us
they have now arranged their finances so that they can go ahead. Last year the subsidy was granted for fifty-one miles, but the survey shows fifty miles, and the present subsidy is for that length.

Is this the company
that owns the coal areas in that county?

I do not know. The
applicants are A. W. Chisholm, Charles E. Sherman, J. D. Taylor, Thomas S. Courtenay, and others.

So far as I am personally concerned, I would like to put on record my belief that the time has come in the history of this country when we should no longer subsidize anything. If public assistance has got to be given for the general benefit of the country, the work with respect to which that assistance is given should be undertaken by the country itself. I wish to place myself on record in that respect, because I firmly believe in that policy, and I hope the day will soon come when shall grant no further subsidies to private parties out of the public treasury.

Resolution agreed to.
To the Northern New Brunswick and Seaboard Railway Company, for a line of railway
from the Drummond Mines at Austin brook, a branch of the Nepisiquit river above Great Falls, in the county of Gloucester, to a point on the Intercolonial railway where it intersects the branch line from Bathurst Station to Bathurst Harbour, in lieu of the subsidy granted by chapter 48 of 1912, section 2, item 24; not exceeding 16.9 miles.

The Government has
decided to dredge out Bathurst harbour, and thus the line will be shortened. The present subsidy is for the shorter length of line.

This will permit the
company to extend their road to Bathurst harbour.
Yes. The Government are dredging Bathurst harbour.
The company have sixteen miles already built.

The road is already
built; but it would have to he extended further if Bathurst harbour is not dredged. It means that much subsidy saved. The line is owned by the Drummonds; it runs out to their mine there.

This company has built their railroad from the mine to the junction of the Intercolonial. That is about sixteen miles, which is in operation, and they are asking for a subsidy from the junction of the Intercolonial railway to Bathurst harbour.

No, this is cutting off a subsidy. The subsidy was granted for twenty-six miles. Now we are having a revote for sixteen and nine-tenths of a^mile. By going to Bathurst harbour, the line is shortened. They can get deeper water by dredging the harbour.

Have they
been paid anything?
No, nothing has been paid yet.

To the Tobique and Campbellton Railway Company, for a line of railway from Plaster-Rock along the Tobique river to Riley brook, in lieu of subsidy granted by chapter 51 of 1910. section 1, item 15; not exceeding 28 miles.
Has anything been done there?

When do they expect

Will the hon. minister give me the names of the directors of the company?

Resolution agreed to.
To the St. John and Quebec Railway Company, for a line of railway from Andover to St. John, New Brunswick, exclusive of a railway bridge across the St. John river, at or near Mistake, and a railway bridge across the Kennebecasis river at or near Perry Point, in lieu of subsidy granted by chapter 46, of 1912, section 2, item 2: not exceeding 200 miles.

I am sorry that the hon. Minister of Railways has not seen fit to grant a subsidy for the construction of this road, not from Andover to St. John but from Grand Falls to St. John. When the late Government was in power, there was an agreement that this road should not be constructed unless it should be built from St. John to Grand Falls. Now for some reason unknown to me, this road is to stop at Andover, a small and rising town on the St. John river, in the county of Victoria. There is every reason for building this road as far as Grand Falls. The country along the St. John river is probably as fertile as any land in Canada. Any railway built along the valley of the St. John river will certainly pay, if it is properly managed. The country from Andover to Grand Falls covers a distance of twenty-five miles. There is on both sides of the river well cultivated and well settled land. The farmers are well off and want transportation facilities for their products. The people of the northern part of New Brunswick want this road built as far as Grand Falls, and they want connections with the Canadian Pacific railway and the National Transcontinental railway there. If the road stops at Andover and runs over the Canadian Pacific railway,
I am afraid there is something behind the scheme that will hurt the progress of the people of the northern part of New Brunswick. It seems to me that the Canadian Pacific railway is going to take over this road. If so, where will competition arise in the way of transportation? At Grand Falls we have a great water-power which is about to be developed. This water-power is held 'by a large company, and I am informed that some of the members of that company are directors of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. If this railroad is not constructed as far as Grand Falls, the connection with the other railways will not. be accomplished. We expect to build a great pulp mill, to develop electricity with this water-power and to provide great industries, not only in the northern part of New Brunswick, but all along the St. John river.
I would, therefore, ask that the minister Mr. COCHRANE.
give us a subsidy, not for two hundred miles, but for two hundred and twenty-five miles, from Grand Falls to St. John.

There is no settled
policy that we shall not build up to Grand Falls; but at present, to say the least, the carrying trade is not very great there. There is an expensive bridge to build and the Canadian Pacific railway run on one side of the river and the St. John and Quebec railway on the other. I know it would accommodate the settlers to have a road on both sides; but we.thought, as the Intercolonial is to run on a forty and a sixty per cent basis, for the present at least it is going to cost more than we can receive until the trade is built up. There is no possibility of getting the road up to Grand Falls in the meantime. Before we ask the House to subsidize the road up to Grand Falls, we should have more information and know definitely what we can get by building this bridge and proceeding twenty-five miles further.

Has the hon. minister
entered into any negotiations with the Canadian Pacific railway as to running rights over the road from Aroostook to Grand Falls?

They approached us
and said they would give us fair running rights there and would be glad to do it as there was scarcely enough space for a road there. I thought we might leave this out in the meantime, and not decide until further information was given.
Does that mean that the Intercolonial railway would take the Canadian Pacific railway from Aroostook junction to Edmundston or only to Grand Falls?

From Andover to
Grand Falls.
It would be in the parish of Andover, but I am satisfied it would not be in the town of Andover.

I am not familiar
enough with the locality to tell my hon. friend.
It does not mean taking the Canadian Pacific railway from Grand Falls to Edmundston.
No, not necessarily.

I am afraid the right
of running over the Canadian Pacific railway from Andover to Grand Falls might interfere with the connection we have with the Canadian Pacific railway, and I hope it will not change anything.

I do not know how
it would interfere. We should run our own trains right up to Grand Falls.

The minister will re-
. member that last .session this Parliament agreed to lend $1,000,000 to the St. John and Quebec railway for the purpose of helping to construct three bridges. If this proposed agreement with the Canadian Pacific railway goes through, it will be unnecessary to construct the Andover bridge.
At present, anyway.
Will the minister pay that $1,000,000 to the company or will he retain a paTt of it?

No, the vote is for
three bridges and we should not have authority to pay it out for only two. We shall have to deduct a portion for the Andover bridge.

I am glad to hear that
statement. But I want to tell the minister that they will be here inside of one month to have that $1,000,000 voted for the two bridges, the Mistake and the Kennebecasis; and more than that, the minister will give it.

The hon. gentleman
may know more than I do, but the minister will not give it.

Well, we have accomplished something. I must say this is the first time I have ever been able to accomplish anything with the Minister of Railways. I am delighted to hear that from him. A year ago, when this legislation was going through, we knew what was going on. We have known for two years that they had no intention of building this road from Andover to Grand Falls. In a small place like New Brunswick the minister will understand, we probably know more about one another's business than do people in a bigger place. My hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Michaud) last session moved an amendment in this House, and it was voted upon, to provide that at least $250,000 should be appropriated to the bridge at Andover, but the minister and his friends voted that down. We knew this was coming; we knew that the St. John and Que-hec Railway Company never intended to go beyond the village of Andover, and we even had some doubts of their going that far. We knew they would go as far as the parish of Andover, but if they are talking about getting running rights over the Canadian Pacific railway, that means that they would go to the village of Andover. But we knew-or believed, at least-that they had no intention of building the bridge. It was to test the matter we moved the amendment, and of course the minister had' it voted down. I am delighted to hear him make the statement that he will not allow them to take all the money on the lower bridges. Will he go so far as to say that
be will reserve a quarter million as we proposed last year?

I could not say that, for, not having 'the report of the engineer, I do not know how it should be divided. I do not know the character .of these streams well enough to give my hon. friend that promise. But it would have to be in proportion to the cost of the three bridges.

That is a fair proposition and I am glad to hear the minister make that statement. Of course, I realize that no man can say that a quarter of a million dollars would be the exact proportion of cost of this bridge, though I believe it is pretty nearly correct. But I am willing to trust the minister when he gives me his word to that extent, that he will carry it out exactly as given.
I do not realize that we have a good thing in this.

No, I do not think the minister has a good thing in this; it is the other fellow who has the good thing. That is exactly what I want to tell him. The other fellow is getting something which no railway company in Canada has ever had before, and which I hope no railway company in Canada will ever get again. I tell the minister that there is nothing in his department that requires looking into so much as this St. John and Quebec Railway Company does. I cannot tell him all I know, but I can tell him enough to make him suspicious, and doing that, I shall accomplish my purpose. When he grows suspicious, and puts a man on the work in whom he has absolute confidence and who will tell him the truth, he will have something to do to straighten out the tangle. The scheme at first was all right; in my judgment it was one of the finest railway schemes proposed in eastern Canada for a long time. The original scheme was that a road should be built from Grand Falls to St. John, passing through a territory that is now without railway communication and making a connecting link to the. city of St. John for the Grand Trunk Pacific traffic. Now, I wish to point out the changes that have been made-not made by the minister, because I do not think he realized what was going on or the extent to which they were departing from the original proposition. Legislation was enacted on the 19th of May, 1911-chapter 11 of the statutes of that year -providing that the Intercolonial railway should have the right to lease this road when constructed and pay forty per cent of the gross earnings over to the company, which money would really go to the government of New Brunswick in so far as it was necessary to pay the interest on the bond guarantee, the balance remaining in the coffers of the company. That road was to be the very best railway which could be
1X675

constructed according to the nature of the country. The clause read:
Provided however that the said contract shall he entered into only upon the condition that the said railway be constructed upon plans and specifications to be approved by the Governor 'in Council upon the recommendation of the Minister of Railways and Canals and shall be up to the standard of the said National Transcontinental through the said province.
Now, the minister knows that the standard of the Transcontinental railway through New Brunswick is the standard of that railway through all the rest of Canada, except that there is one place from Plaster Rock eastward for about fourteen miles where they have a pusher grade of 1 -10 per cent. Except for that, the general make-up of the road, the width of embankments, width of cuts, curvatures, alignment, grades, station houses, rails, ties, fastenings [DOT]-everything that makes a road, is of the highest standard known in Canada; and the road we proposed building was to be up to that standard. But we have to admit that it would be necessary to depart from that standard so far as grades are concerned, because the standard of the Transcontinental in New Brunswick admitted of higher grades, though only in one place where it was absolutely necessary. In other words, we proposed a road which would be a real extension of the Grand Trunk Pacific to St. John and make the outlet to the Grand Trunk Pacific business for the port of St. John. Now, hon. gentlemen opposite came into power, and I will show the minister what this did. They passed an Act, chapter 49 of the statutes of 1912, and whoever drew that statute drew it very cunningly. The whole difficulty rests in the provisions of section 10, which is as follows:
Notwithstanding anything in any other Act, the agreement set out in the schedule to this Act is hereby ratified and confirmed and declared to be binding upon the respective parties thereto, subject to the provisions of this Act, and the Dominion may do whatever is necessary to give full effect to the said agreement and specifications to the provisions of this Act.
It will be seen that by this section the Act of 1911, which provided not for a tramway but for a railway, was entirely discarded. Then they proceed to ratify and affirm the provisions of an agreement attached to the Act as a schedule. Section 2 of the agreement is as follows:
That the company shall complete the construction and equipment of the said railway in all respects up to and according to the specifications hereto annexed and the requirements as in the preceding clause set out on or before the first day of November, in the year of our Lord one thousand nine hundred and fifteen.	i
Mr. CARVELL.
But there is no schedule attached, and the result of that legeislation was that the minister absolutely abrogated the provisions of the Act of 1911. He makes law an agreement made between the railway company and the province of New Brunswick, in which it is stated that the specifications shall conform with the specifications in the schedule attached to the agreement, but no specifications are to be found. The whole matter was left wide open, and these people were free to do as they pleased.
It would amaze the hon. minister if he knew what they were doing. I know that the St. John Standard to-morrow will come . out with great headlines to the effect that Mr. Carvell is opposing the construction of the Valley railway, and all the lesser lights will do the same thing; but I consider that I have a duty to perform, and I intend to perform it. I wish to put the minister on his guard; I wish to acquaint him with the facts, and if he is not sufficiently interested to investigate the matter, I at least will have done my duty. I tell the minister and tap the Grand Trunk Pacific; other-word I know that will express the condition of affairs that exists. The only justification for the construction of that road under the conditions under which it is beipg constructed would be to go to JGrand Falls and tap the Grand Trunk Pacific; otherwise the minister was never justified, in making the contract which he did make. We are giving these people a subsidy of $6,400 a mile; the province of New Brunswick is giving them a bond guarantee of $25,000 a mile, and they are therefore receiving $31,400 a mile of public assistance. The Intercolonial is leasing that road, and paying back to the company 40 cents out of every dollar,,no matter-how much it costs to earn it. The minister is right in saying that this is a wonderful contract. It would be absolutely justified if we had a railroad connecting two competing points; a railroad which could get business, and which could handle the business lf it did get it. But the kind of Toad the minister is getting cannot get business, and could not handle it if it did. In my judgment the Government are going to suffer an enormous loss in the operation of this road. It they had carried out the original arrangement and built a road according to the standard provided in 1911, the results would have been satisfactory, and even if they had tapped the Grand Trunk Pacific at Grand Falls, sixty per cent would have paid runing expenses, the people would have got the benefit of it, and the Inter! colonial would not lose any money. It may ' be said that I am opposed to the local Gov; ernment of New Brunswick and opposed to [ this Government, and that I am trying to ; find fault. It is true that I am opposed to

the Government, but it is not true that I am trying to find fault. I am just as anxious to see the railroad built through that country as is any person in the province of New Brunswick. This railroad passes my home, where my mother and brothers live, and where our property is situated. The presence of the railroad increases the value of the property, and I therefore have a personal interest in its operation. It runs through fifty miles of my constituency, and it will provide railway facilities for the people throughout the whole of that district. I am interested privately and publicly; I want to see the road go through, but I want to see it go through in such shape that it will redound to the benefit of the people and not be a sink-hole for the funds of the Government that tries to operate it. I am not alone in my protest in regard to this matter. I call in evidence a member of this House who feels just as strongly over this matter as I do; a gentleman who perhaps is not in a position to protest as lustily as I do, but who is just as much interested in the matter, and who realizes just as well as I do the iniquity of this proposition. I refer to the hon. member for York, N.B. (Mr. Crocket). I have in my hand a return brought down by the minister; and I want to read the first public protest received from one of his friends with regard to the character of the roads they are building in the province of New Brunswick. It is in the form of a telegram. and is as follows:
Fredericton, N.B., July 11, 1912.
A. W. Campbell, C.E.,
Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals, Ottawa.
Construction is now proceeding on St. John and Quebec railway location which has been condemned by Dominion inspecting engineer. Think you should intimate to company that location must be approved before construction is proceeded with and that your department will not consider itself bound in reference to subsidy by approval of local government. Understand there is no need of any seven degree curve between here and St. John, yet company's plans show great number. There is one of them on one of the highest fills on the road within two miles of Fredericton on which construction is now proceeding.
Oswald S. Crocket.
I submit that my hon. friend did his duty; he pointed out to the minister what was going on at the earliest stages, before the plans had been approved, and before the construction of the road had been commenced. This was followed by a protest on the part of Mr. Sherwood, the chief engineer, who points out dozens of places in respect of which in his judgment the plans should be revised and made to conform to a proper standard. His letter may be found in this return under date of July 25; I have not time to read it, but I desire to call my hon. friend's attention to it.
He will find that at eight different points they put in 7-degree curves which his own engineers deemed unnecessary. The engineer pointed out dozens of things that were not necessary, but they have all come to pass. The St. John and Quebec Railway Company owns the Government of New Brunswick and owns the Government of Canada, and they are able to do whatever they please. Every objection urged by the Government engineer, Mr. Sherwood, was simply brushed aside, and the company went on to complete the road according to their own wishes. There was some dispute just below Fredericton as to the location of the road; whether it should go along the river where the people lived, or whether it should go back among the hills. In this matter the company won out; as they always do. They fought it out for a year, but the company won out, as they always do, and they tried to show, as I find by this return, that it would cost more to build a railway along the river than to put it out where nobody lives. It would cost only $16,000 a mile to build the road up to subgrade, even in the expensive places, and not more than half of that in the other places, and this company has received $31,000; and yet, with a confession like that, my hon. friend's department allows them in the end to have their way and go back in the woods and build a cheap road. They agreed that the road from Fredericton to St. John should have no greater grade against eastbound traffic than .4 per cent and against westbound traffic of .6 per cent. But there came a place where they had to cross a creek, just below Fredericton. This is a small creek which it would cost a few hundred or a thousand dollars more to bridge if they built it to grade, and a few thousand dollars to build the approaches if they were built up to grade; yet they asked permission of the Government to change the grade at that point. Mr. Taylor, the department engineer in New Brunswick, who, I judge, is a conscientious man and anxious to do right, is over-ruled in every case. My hon. friend's department came in, and they are putting in nearly a one per cent grade over this creek, a velocity grade, they call it, down one hill and up another and over the bridge in order to avoid building the road up to the proper standard. Yet they received $31,400 per mile of public money. That is south of Fredericton where they are supposed to be building a .4 per cent grade one way and a .6 per cent grade another way. My hon. friend should go north of Fredericton to see these people doing business in their own Yankee style. I do not know that my hon. friend is responsible for this, but his friends are. Of all the people -willing to build that railroad no

man would be listened to, let alone contracted with, except a shrewd Yankee named Gould, from the state of Maine, a bright fellow and a man against whom I have not a word to say. I rather admire a man who has sand enough to come over and clean up the whole province of New Brunswick, and I tell my hon. friends he will go away with $500,000 of clean, cold cash. There was no man on earth to whom they would talk except Mr. Gould, and they finally signed a contract with him, and he has them just where he wants them, he is doing up both this Government and the Government of New Brunswick.
Is it not the same company you were doing business with?
Not by any means.
Oh, yes.
Oh, but I know better. I do not want to say that offensively, but I am so positive that I am compelled to use pretty strong language.
My department informs me to that effect.

My hon. friend the
Minister of Railways is referring to an
agreement made in 1911 before he came into power; but that agreement was entered into when the local Government of New Brunswick would not agree with anybody else.
I do not know that.

We all know it in New Brunswick. We know that the local Government would not even talk to anybody else. My hon. friend knows that Mr. Malcolm made an offer to take the bond guarantee and subsidy and build the road under the legislation we passed in 1911, and to build a railroad and not a tranrway; they treated him with contempt and laughed at him. I repeat that the only man they would consider for a moment was this Vankee, Gould, and they have got him and he has got them. The file is not nearly complete, because I have seen myself letters from Mr. Taylor ordering the contractors on that road north of Fredericton to stop work because he would not approve of the grades and curvatures. The work was stopped for two or three weeks, the contractors being held up; but finally Mr. Taylor was turned down and they went on, and. put in seven-degree curves the same as before and gradients the same as before. More than that, there were no specifications put in this legislation; and so the Government have agreed, by Order in Council, that they shall put in seven-degree curves wherever they want to and one per cent grades wherever they want to. I can take the minister to places in Carle-Mr. CARVELL.	:
ton-I have been on the ground myself, and I have seen plans and profiles that Show four seven-degree curves in one and one-quarter miles on a one per cent grade- and the minister talks about transporting freight over a road like that. I find in one of these documents a confession from the company themselves. When the Government engineer was trying to make them put on certain track fastenings to make the road safer from a transportation standpoint, and the company objected, they said:	Over thirty per cent of our
road is on curvatures, and less than seventy per cent is on tangents, and if you ask us to straighten up the rails on curvatures, you will make us spend too much money. The Yankee has had his' way every time he has gone up against the minister. I point to a dozen instances, and every time the Yankee comes up to the minister he wins.
That is more than the rest of us can do.

I do not know how it
is, but he does it just the same; he puts in any grade he wants. If he wants the grade changed from four-tenths of one per cent to one per cent he can get it; he can get the road placed in the woods when it should be on the river; he can get as many seven-degree curves to the mile as he wants, and Mr. Taylor can object to his heart's content, and it amounts to nothing; Mr. Gould goes on and does as he has a mind to. I am not finding fault with Mr. Gould; he is a bright, shrewd man, a real gentleman to meet, a man who is getting from the Government of this country and of New Brunswick, as I said, $31,400 a mile for building a railway, and he is building simply a tramway. I make the statement to the minister now, and I want him to send some competent engineer over the road, with a knowledge of the statements I am making to him, that the railroad that these people are building from Fredericton to Centreville, for eighty-five miles that I know of, which I have gone over personally, is not costing, complete, $20,000 a mile, including bridges and everything else. I cannot go further that that, but I give my hon. friend the tip to go to the contractors and subcontractors, and to take the plans and profiles in his office, and comoare them with the actual conditions on the ground. He will then see whether I have not been doing my duty in calling his attention to the matter. You ask why I am doing this. I am doing it because, in the first place, I wanted this to be a railroad, and I worked for it five or six years. It was practically the one local road I have had in view almost since I was in politics. The Grand Trunk Pacific should neveT

have gone through the centre of New Brunswick. I agree with my hon friend the minister, and with the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) in that. I made that statement when my friends were in power, and if my hon. friend from St. Anto-ine would take the trouble to look up some remarks of mine, made in 1905-06, he would find that what I have said is correct. It should have gone down the St. John river to Fredericton and across to Moncton. You would only have increased the mileage by twenty or twenty-five miles, you would have had a much better railroad, and I do not think it would have cost so much as the present one. However, when I could not get what I wanted, I determined if posible to get a railway through that country. Whether my efforts had anything to do with it or not, I do not know, but the road is being built now, and I am glad of it. I am only sorry that we are not getting the kind of railway we should have got. I am bringing this to t*he attention of the minister bee a use the country is suffering, and because the Intercolonial is suffering. My hon. friend has to operate this railway, he has to pay back forty cents out of every dollar to this company, and as nearly as I can figure it out this company is going to make three-quarters of a million dollars in cold cash on the line to Andover. I realize the importance of the statement I am making. I know I am going to be pounded by every Conservative newspaper in New Brunswick, and that I shall meet this thing a good many times during the next few months. But I am doing my duty in pointing out the exact condition of affairs, which my hon. friend can find out for himself if he goes there and looks over the ground. I hope my hon. friend will do himself the justice of going there, or of sending someone in whom he has confidence, and if he does so, he will find a condition of affairs which he would hardly conceive possible. I am not casting any insinuations at anybody; I do not know who is to blame, but there seems to be someone high up in authority, who is allowing these people to build the kind of road they are building. As I said before, every time this shrewd Yankee runs up against the Department of Railways and Canals, he wins out, and you have proof of the fact in this document. There are to my knowledge, other proofs which do not exist in that document. It is not tgo late even now to remedy some of those defects. I do not believe there is a spot on that railroad where it was possible to put in one per cent grade * that they have not done so. They have made seven degree curves for the sake of getting rid of a few hundred dollars worth of material, when the road might as well have been made straight. Every device known to engineers
has been resorted to upon that work to make it valueless as a transportation proposition. It is unique; I think there is no road in the Dominion to-day-perhaps that is putting it too strongly-but I do not know of a railway to-day which pretends to be a transportation proposition that has the -curves and grades that this railway has.
As to the proposition of my hon. friend to lease the Canadian Pacific railway, I wish he would go into that matter carefully. It is true he will not get a great amount of business from Andover to Grand * Falls, -but the intention was to cross the river at Andover, and to give the people on the other side railway facilities which they do not have at present. It would be a very great boon to those people, and a great benefit to that portion of the province. But the real object of this road being built to Grand Falls was, as I have pointed out, to get the freight traffic from the Grand Trunk Pacific. My hon. friend will find that he can never do business profitably over the twenty-four miles which he proposes to lease from the Canadian Pacific railway. It is, without doubt, the poorest railrpad in the province, from a transportation standpoint. It is true that the Canadian Pacific railway have improved the road bed; they have put in culverts and the road is now in pretty good shape; but they have two grades on that twenty-four mile stretch which are simply impossible for transportation purposes. I have not the figures before me, but my hon. friend will find the first grade about half-way between Aroostook junction and Grand Falls, and the next one just before he comes to Grand Falls. I do not know how steep they are, but they are enormous, and away above everything that any railway pretending to be a transportation proposition should have. There is one place where they must climb a hill of one hundred feet, when they could have gone along on the level. But it was said yeaTs ago that it was only a question of building a road, and of getting 10,000 acres of land from the province. They built the kind of road that Mr. Gould is building for the Minister of Railways. He is getting $31,400 per mile for building that road, and the cheaper the road he builds, the more money goes into his pocket. It was just the same with the old New Brunswick company.
Why do you not join me in opposing subsidies?

The railway which he is proposing to lease from the Canadian Pacific railway never was, and never can be, a transportation proposition. On motion of Mr. Cochrane, House went into Committee to consider certain proposed resolutions respecting the granting of the subsidies therein mentioned towards certain lines of railway of the Canadian Northern Railway Company (see Debates, pp. 11326-11327.)
(Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)

In the legislation now before fthe House it is proposed to extend further aid to the Canadian Northern railway in connection with the 'building of its Transcontinental line from Montreal to Vancouver, and, also, to the important feeder to its main line between Ottawa and Toronto. The aid proposed is in the form of a cash subsidy at the rate of $12,000 per mile from Ottawa (to Port Arthur, and also for the same amount per mile from Edmonton to the Yellowhead Pass, and an amount of $6,400 per mile on the main feeder from Toronto to Ottawa, as follows:	Ottawa to
Port Arthur-nine hundred and ten miles, at $12,000 per mile, $10,920,000; Edmonton to Yellowhead Pass-two hundred and sixty miles, at $12,000 per mile, $3,120,000; Toronto to Ottawa-two hundred and fifty miles, at $6,400 per mile, $1,600,000-$15,-640,000.
A condition to the granting of the aforesaid aid is that the company are to transfer to the Government Canadian Northern railway common stock to the par value of $7,000,000. This common stock, although not on the market at the present time, has considerable value, and there is no doubt that after the completion of the undertaking it will be a valuable asset to the Dominion.
There is nothing applying to the subsidy of $6,400 per mile for the Toronto to Ottawa line calling for any special remarks, as this is the usual subsidy granted to practically all railway companies when the cost is equal to or exceeds $21,400 per mile. The estimated cost is $41,131 per mile.
On the Ottawa to Port Arthur line the construction is of a most expensive charac-
369i
ter, and the estimated average cost per mile is $49,381. The Government have already aided this section of the line by guaranteeing the three and a half per cent bonds issued by the company to an amount of $35,000 per mile, but the company have only been able to dispose of these bonds at the rate of ninety and three-fourtihs cents on the dollar, which has produced $31,760 per mile.
On the line from Edmonton to Yellowhead Pass the construction is also of. a very expensive nature. This section of the line has already been aided by the guaranteeing of the company's three and a half per cent bonds to the extent of $13,000 per mile starting at St. Albert thence westerly fifty miles; and from that point westerly for one hundred miles at the Tate of $25,000 per mile, and for the last one hundred and two miles westerly to the Yellowhead Pass at the rate of $35,000 per mile. These bonds were disposed of at an average of eighty-seven cents on the dollar; which produced $22,400 per mile.
The average cost of the line is estimated at $38,500 per mile. In other words, taking the line from Ottawa to Port Arthur and from Edmonton to Yellowhead pass; the company have financed to the amount of approximately $34,578,220, and are faced with a construction charge of $54,638,981. The aid now proposed on the above sections will amount to $14,040,000.
The question naturally arises as to the reasons which would justify the Government in granting this aid, and as to whether in granting the aid they are assisting this great Transcontinental line to a greater extent than the other two transcontinental lines of Canada. Careful consideration was given to this before the legislation brought down was approved, and the conclusion reached was that the Government, having regard to all the circumstances, were only dealing fairly with the Canadian Northern railway in granting them this aid. A comparison with that granted the Canadian Pacific railway cannot fairly be made, as the assistance rendered that road was on altogether a different basis. The land grant given the Canadian Pacific railway in the light of later developments was a tremendous bonus; but at the time it was not generally considered to be a very valuable asset. The money grants and the construction of certain sections of the road by the Government appeared at the time to be a large figure; but we must bear in mind that it was the pioneer road, and that little was known of the country it traversed.
A fair comparison as to aid given would be that granted the Grand Trunk Pacific railway for the construction of its main line from Winnipeg to Prince Rupert, and also

the terms and conditions in connection with 'the leasing of the eastern section from Winnipeg to Moncton, which is being built by the Government. The western division of the Transcontinental railway, which is owned and equipped by the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, is divided into two sections -the prairie section from Winnipeg to the east bank of the Wolf creek, a distance of nine hundred and fifteen miles, and the mountain section, from that point to prince Rupert, a distance of eight hundred and thirty-five miles.
The Prairie Section has been aided by a guarantee of bonds to the amount of $13,000 per mile, and in addition by a loan of $10,000,000.
The Mountain Section had been aided by a guarantee of bonds to the amount of seventy-five per cent of the actual cost of the road; and the cost of Ike Mountain Section is estimated to be $80,306 per mile; the guarantee will, therefore, average $60,229 per mile. A further aid to the Western Division was an implementing clause in the agreement between the company and the Government, whereby the Government was to pay the company the difference be-twen the par value of the bonds and the actual amount they produced. This has been estimated to amount, on the total guarantee, to $13,000,000; and there has been paid on this account $4,994,416. Latterly the Government has adopted the policy of purchasing the bonds themselves at par; but if they had made the whole purchase and then put them on the market there is no doubt that the amount realized would have been $13,000,000 short of the par value.
In addition to the above, the Government is to pay the interest upon an amount of bonds equal to the principal of the bonds guaranteed by the Government on account of the construction of the Mountain Section accruing during the first seven years. Estimating the cost of the Mountain Section as $67,056,000, the interest will amount to a cash subsidy of $10,561,321.
In respect to the Eastern Section, the Government is to build the same and lease it to the company at an annual rental based on three per cent of the cost. The estimated cost of this section, seven years from date road is completed, is $230,000,000. Based on this amount, the annual rental would be $'6,900,000. But there is another item which must be taken into consideration. In the first
place, I must express my disappointment at the meagreness of the reasons why my hon. friend has given to the House for this new aid to the Canadian Northern Railway Company. There is no disposition on this side of the House to view critically the legislation which has been introduced on the present occasion to grant assistance to that company in their enterprise of constructing a third transcontinental railway. Parliament has already subsidized that enterprise, and subsidized it upon terms which we thought to be generous and adequate to carry it to completion. So far as I have been able to follow his statement, the only reason given by my hon. friend why this additional assistance should be given to the company, is that it has not been assisted in the past so generously as the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Pacific railway. I am sorry that the memorandum which has just been Tead by my hon. friend was not placed on the table earlier. When he gave notice of this resolution, I asked him to bring down all the correspondence, and to furnish, in advance, all the information that he had in his hands, so as to facilitate the discussion. My hon. friend told me then that there was no correspondence with the company-
That is right.

-that all the negotiations had been verbal. It seems to me that, since the company were asking such generous assistance, the Government would have done better to have asked them for a statement of the reasons which had brought them to the door of the Government for more assistance. It would
have been more satisfactory to the Government, to Parliament, and to the people, if the company had put those reasons in black and white. But since there has been no correspondence, we have to guess what the reasons may be. The only reason which has been disclosed. by my hon. friend up to the present time-and if I am in error he will correct ame-the only reason he disclosed in the memorandum which he read, and which I presume came from the company, was that the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific had been assisted upon a more generous scale than the Canadian Northern Railway Company. But I submit that that is no reason whatever. It must be apparent to everybody that, as a country develops, railway construction must become less and less expensive. The construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific could not 'be as expensive as that of the Canadian Pacific railway, and the construction of the Canadian Northern railway could not be as expensive as that of the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company was the pioneer company, which had to carry its supplies and everything else through an unsettled country, and therefore the cost of construction must have been much heavier. When, later on, the Grand Trunk Pacific was constructed, that company had the benefit of the existing railway, the Canadian Pacific railway, and the cost of construction must have been very much less than that of the Canadian Pacific railway. When the third transcontinental railway, built by the Canadian Northern Railway Company, was proceeded with, it had the advantage of the two existing roads, over which it could carry its supplies. Apart from the one consideration, that labour may be dearer now than it was at the time the Canadian Pacific railway was built, although perhaps not much dearer than when the Grand Trunk Pacific was built, the conditions are to the advantage of the Canadian Northern. Canada has gone into the construction of railways on a scale up-precedented in any country. We were forced to do this on account of our proximity to the United States; we could not wait until private enterprise alone would provide the railway facilities which this new country required, and out of the bounty of the Government we aided private enterprise. But as time goes on and the country is developed, railway construction will less and less require aid from the public treasury.
The only reason given by my hon. friend so far for this proposal, is that he wants to equalize the assistance given to this road with the assistance given another road. That is no reason whatever for this legislation. The question is first, whether the enterprise is worthy of assistance, and,,

then, whether or not the company is able to carry on its enterprise. My hon. friend would not only have done well, but I submit that it was his -duty, first of all to give us a statement of the financial position of this company, so that we might judge whether the demand was justified or not. In 1884, when the Canadian Pacific railway was under construction, the company knocked at the door of Parliament for aid, and it was given. But they gave us a statement of their reasons for asking for aid, stating that they could not carry on the enterprise and that it would have to collapse if assistance were not given. If the Canadian Northern Company had now given us some reason of that kind, and had shown us that they were not in a condition to carry on their enterprise, I could understand the application which is made. But, as it is, we have to take a leap in the dark, and the only reason given is one which for my part I cannot entertain, and which I do not believe Parliament will entertain.
If this railroad has to be assisted, how are we to assist it? We have already subsidized this company to a large extent from Ottawa to the boundary of British Columbia, by endorsation of its bonds to the amount of $35,000 per mile. As to the section in British Columbia, from the Yellowhead pass to the Pacific ocean, we gave it last year a cash subsidy of $12,000 per mile, and in addition it has a subsidy from the province of British Columbia. It will therefore be seen that the company has already been generously subsidized. The only point, after all for us to consider is this: if it requires assistance, what should the nature of that assistance be? I believe the days have passed when an enterprise of this kind should be aided by a cash subsidy. We have not done it in the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and there is no reason why we should do it in the case of this railway. If any assistance is to be given to the company, it should be by way of loan and not by way of cash subsidy.	-
Looking back upon the history of railway legislation in Canada, we must come to the conclusion that the Government of the day would have shown more foresight, and would have acted more in the public interest, had it assisted the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in 1881 with a loan rather than with the enormous cash subsidy we gave it. The fact is that at present, if the Canadian Pacific railway is suffering from anything, it is from a plethora of wealth. We have subsidized the Canadian Pacific Railway Company lavishly. I do not say that by way of recrimination; it may be, and I believe it is so, that at that time the Canadian Pacific railway would not have been built had it not been for the extravagant terms we gave to the company. But now that we have before us Sir WILFRID LA DRIER.
the result of the operations of The Canadian Pacific railway, we see that it would have been far better in the public interest had we done as the United States did in the case of the Union Pacific, namely, lent the credit of the Government to that enterprise instead of giving it a cash subsidy. To-day the very wealth of the Canadian Pacific railway is, I will not say a danger, but an obstacle in the way of the adjustment of freight rates on the roads of other companies. It is easy to be wise after the event; I do not recriminate; but if in 1881 we had loaned to the Canadian Pacific railway $150,000,000 to carry on its enterprise, to-day the whole of that money could have been recouped, to the advantage of the company and of the Canadian people. We did not do so; but to-day we can learn a lesson and take heed, from our remissness in the past.
Instead of giving this cash .subsidy of $158,000,000 out of the treasury to the Canadian Northern, I ask my hon. friend why in the very next resolution on the Order PapeT he proposes to grant help to the Grand Trunk Pacific by way of a loan. What reason is there for giving a cash subsidy to the one railway and a loan to the other? Would not the public interest be better served if we followed the same rule in both cases? Would not the enterprise be benefited just as well if we were to loan to the Canadian Northern Company the $15,000,000 which it wants, just as we are loaning to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company the money it wants? Let me call the attention of the House to the resolution with respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific:
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide for and to authorize an advance out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund by way of loan te the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company of a sum not exceeding fifteen million dollars, for the purpose of assisting the company in completing the western division of its railway; such advance to be repayable with interest half-yearly at the rate of four per centum per annum, not later than July 1, 1923, the advance to be secured by debentures charged upon the western division of the company's railway, and upon the undertaking, equipment and property, rights and franchises of the company, ranking next after the debenture stock of the company issued or to be issued under chapter 100 of the Acts of 1906, and the Act respecting the company assented to on the seventh day of March, 1913, such debentures to be guaranteed, both as to principal and interest, by the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada.
Let me ask now why, in giving aid to these two transcontinental railways, which are both in the process of construction, one mode of help is given to one and another mode of help is given to the other. What reason has. impelled the

Government to give a loan of $15,000,000 to one and a cash subsidy to the other?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is a very proper question, which my right hon. friend asks, and I am confident that the Government is able to make a reply which will satisfy this House and the people of this country. The policy of granting subsidies to railway companies, and especially to railway companies engaged in the task of building transcontinental lines, is not new. It is as old as Confederation and has been forced upon every government of this country by the facts and exigencies which have confronted us, principally owing to our geographical position and the extent and character of the country which must be traversed by the lines which bind Canada together from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
Canada is divided into four parts. Political confederation would not have been possible except by binding together the isolated sections of Canada. That was recognized at the time of Confederation, and the Intercolonial had to be built in order to join up the maritime provinces with Quebec and Ontario. We have between the province of Ontario and the prairie provinces a stretch of about a thousand miles of almost barren wilderness that must be linked up by railway lines in order that the Ontario and the East may have access to the prairie provinces. Similarly, when you traverse the prairie provinces, you come to the great barrier of the Rocky mountains that shuts off the prairie provinces from British Columbia. The task that has been set to every government of Canada is how to provide transportation facilities for the people of Canada. We have an area in this Dominion the size of Europe. We have almost four thousand miles to traverse from coast to coast. We have to the south of us a republic from which our people have been shut off by a hostile tariff. Therefore the problem has been and is to-day, in a larger degree than anything else, the problem of transportation. That was felt at the period to which my right hon. friend refers, the period of the building of the Canadian Pacific line, which was heavily subsidized was built. That condition existed in 1903, and subsequently, when my right hon. friend inaugurated the great enterprises of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. That problem exists to-day with regard to all these lines, and any new lines that may be necessary in order to serve the requirerhents of the country.
My right hon. friend has spoken as if railway subsidies were an entirely new idea. No doubt most of us would agree that if we could avoid it, it would be inadvisable to give money to railway companies, no matter upon what terms, in consideration of their building railways. As a matter of
fact, the principle of railway subsidies is as old as Canada and it is with us to-day. My right hon. friend had to deal with it with regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific railway and in the numerous subsidy Bills which he has brought down. I am surprised that he should express the views that he has put forward to-day as to the propriety of giving railway subsidies, especially in connection with transcontinental lines. They are not ordinary lines; they have to be built, as I have said, along the north shore of lake Superior and through the Rocky mountains where the cost of construction is immense, so that no railway company could be expected to build those lines without substantial assistance from the Government of Canada.
Let me take up by way of illustration the different transcontinental lines that have been subsidized and assisted, and that have built their lines from the Atlantic to the Pacific. In the first place, take the Canadian Pacific railway, and I agree with my right hon. friend that conditions are different now. There were difficulties in the way of getting supplies for the building of the Canadian Pacific railway. If that is so in the West, so far as the East is concerned the cost of building transcontinental lines has increased enormously since the time when the Canadian Pacific railway was built. It is a fair setoff, one against the other. The difficulties of the Rocky mountains are the same now as they were then. So far as eastern Ontario and Quebec are concerned, we all know the cost of building railway lines has increased enormously. The cost of acquiring railway terminals runs into tremendous sums. This is common knowledge. What did the Canadian Pacific railway get? They got $25,000,000 in cash; they got 25,000,000 acres of land which have turned out to be worth a greater sum than the capital stock of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I shall not take it on the basis of to-day's value; I shall deal with it on the basis at which it was deemed proper it should be taken at that time. The 25,000,000 acres of land were stated to be worth from $1 to $1.50 an acre. With the development of this land, which has been brought about not only by the Canadian Pacific railway, but by all these other railway companies which have been built, it has turned out to be worth a sum in excess of $250,000,000. What else did they get? They got in addition to that 700 miles of completed line of railway from Prince Arthur's landing to a point west of Winnipeg, 500 miles; and from Port Moody east thmugh the Fraser canyon, 200 miles. They got all these grants from the Dominion Government in consideration of their undertaking to build the line. What would that subsidy amount to at that time? It is the very opposite of

a mile was given to this company in respect of its line from Toronto to Sudbury1 to connect with the main line. The Canadian Northern Railway Company applied for a subsidy and not for a loan, for the reasons I have mentioned. In addition to the enormous sums of money which private enterprise has supplied, the Government steps in and does, not something new, not something novel, but something which the Government of Canada has always been obliged to do, namely, contribute from the Dominion funds by way of subsidies, the consideration to the Dominion being the advantage which will accrue to the people of Canada by the construction of a transcontinental line. I think there has been a misconception on the part of my right hon. friend, or rather he has not turned his mind upon the matter. I must say he does not misconceive very many things; he is exceedingly well posted with regard to every aspect of Canadian affairs, but I think he has failed to recognize the enormous project which the Canadian Northern Railway Company has in hand, and how much that project means to the people of Canada.
The Canadian Northern railway system is divided into two sections. The western -section extends from Port Arthur to Edmonton, and comprises the network of lines in the provinces of Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan. They have a line running from Winnipeg to Duluth, carrying the grain of the West to that port. The Canadian Northern Railway Company carries between thirty and forty per cent of the grain of the West. Under their enterprising president and vice-president they have built or acquired over a mile of railway a day since 1898. Fifteen thousand men are engaged on the Canadian Northern railr way construction, and twenty-five thousand in connection with the operation of the line. They have forty-five hundred miles of railway in the West, and eighteen hundred miles of railway in the East. The eastern division consists of the Canadian Northern Ontario and the Canadian Northern Quebec railways, the Canadian Northi-ern Ontario comprising the line running from Toronto to Sudbury, the proposed line from Toronto to Ottawa, the line from Ottawa to Montreal, and the proposed line to the Niagara frontier from Toronto. In Quebec the Canadian Northern has acquired the Great Northern and the Quebec and St. John railway, and has linked up the cities of Quebec and Montreal.
Is it the intention to link up with the Quebec and Saguenay railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am entirely unable to answer my hon. friend; I have no knowledge of the matter to which he refers. We Mr. WHITE (Leeds!
are speaking now of the linking up of the city of Quebec with Vancouver, because that is the project of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. As I have said the Canadian Northern Railway Company plays an important part in the transportation problems of the Dominion. It must be borne in mind that we are dealing with subsidies in respect of the main line between Ottawa and Port Arthur, Edmonton and Summit, and Toronto and Ottawa. We are dealing with the main line only. It must be thoroughly borne in mind at the outset, that what we are doing is giving a subsidy in conformity with the policy that has always obtained, a subsidy to a main transcontinental line.	,
As I have said, the Canadian Northern railway have done a very great deal of development work in the Canadian Northwest. My hon. friend knows as well as anyone what a part they played in settling the Saskatchewan valley, in bringing in immigration from United States and from Great Britain. Then they have, in addition to the Canadian Northern itself, various other lines, for instance, the Royal Steamship line, which is a subsidiary company, its bonds and stocks owned by the Canadian (Northern railway. Similarly they have terminal elevators at Port Arthur, and numerous other subsidiary enterprises, telegraph and express companies, all owned by the Canadian Northern railway in connection with their enterprise from East to West. It has been frequently said in public, and I only refer to this fact in order to remove any misconception, that the Canadian Northern has really built its line out of provincial and Dominion guarantees.
In passing, let me say that, so far as a guarantee is concerned-and I quote the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) as to this on numerous occasions -the liability is contingent; the Dominion lends its credit to a railway company. My hon. friends opposite have said on various occasions that it was not expected at all that the Government would be called upon to pay under those guarantees; a guarantee is a contingent liability, the company asks the Dominion to lend it its credit and in connection with a transcontinental line, which properly comes within Dominion jurisdiction and serves the purpose of the entire Dominion. I take no exception, speaking for myself, to the principle of giving Dominion aid by way of guarantee, provided that it is properly secured, and provided it can be shown that it is in the interest of the people of the Dominion as a whole that it should be done, and that a powerful railway company or group are prepared to build and operate a railway line which will inure to the benefit of the people of Canada.

Let me refer to the cost of the Canadian Northern system. I looked into it not long ago because, as Minister of Finance, I felt that I was interested in these matters when granting subsidies to the Canadian Northern, just as I was interested in the loan to the Grand Trunk Pacific. I find that the entire cost of the Canadian Northern system, the parent company and the eastern division, comprising the railways I have mentioned, is no less a sum than $265,000,000 to date. That is the cost of the Canadian Northern railway system. Securities guaranteed by Government, Dominion and provincial, of which I can furnish details, have been issued to the extent of $120,000,000, that is securities which provided $120,000,000, and the Canadian Northern Railway Company, by the issue of their own securities, their perpetual debenture stock, land grant and other bonds, have made issues that have realized $145,000,000, principally of English money. The guarantee of securities by the Dominion and, by the provinces to the extent
of $120,000,000 was a most valuable aid, but, as I have pointed out, this liability of the Dominion and of the provinces is contingent, it is not direct, and therefore, so long as the Canadian Northern as a going concern is able to pay its interest, the Dominion will not be called upon and cannot be called upon to pay any part of the interest; the Dominion has loaned its credit only.
Mr. MACDONALD. That does not include subsidies?

The contracts call for the completion of the line by the end of this year, 1913, and it is estimated that by the summer of next year, if the same conditions prevail as have prevailed as to labour, the Canadian Northern Railway Company will be running trains across the continent from Quebec to the Pacific coast. At all events that is what they have in view, what they hope and expect. Now, what is the assistance that has been received on this main line, because I shall centre my attention on the main line. I have shown, I think to the satisfaction of the House, that no transcontinental line, either in the remote past or in the recent past, has been, or could be built in this country without Dominion subsidies. As I have said, we may theoretically object to subsidies, but we are confronted with a condition, and not a theory. My right hon. friend was unable to project a transcontinental railway across this continent without granting vast subsidies, giving immense guarantees, and making large loans, and if that had to be done in 1903 and 1909, I do not think that the situation has materially changed to-day. I think it was estimated by the hon. member for South Renfrew, then Minister of Railways, that that section was to cost from $50,000 to $55,000 a mile to complete and equip. On the recommendation of my hon. friend the member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), the Government of my right hon. friend introduced legislation whereby the bonds of the Canadian Northern Ontario Company-because that is the only company that owns the line-were guaranteed to the extent of $35,000 per mile, the line, as I have said, costing, on the estimate of the then Minister of Railways, from $50,000 to $55,000 a mile. The proceeds of that guarantee-because the three and one-half per cent stock did not sell at par-was $31,762 per mile, so that to make it perfectly plain, the line, which, on the estimate of my hon. friend, would cost from $50,000 to $55,000 per mile, received a Dominion guarantee which produced $31,000 per mile, leaving $24,000 per mile to be raised by the promoters of the road and $24,000 per mile for a thousand miles is $24,000, a vast sum. I want to give the figures fully and frankly. They received from the Ontario Government a land grant of 4,000 acres per mile, amounting to
2,000,000 acres for the line from Selwood to Port Arthur. That land may become valuable, and I have no doubt it will, but it has not assisted them in the construction of their line, and in the nature of things it could not, because'it is not yet open to settlement.
Let me add one thing more-because it is precisely analagous to what we are doing to-day. The Government of my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier)-I desire to be corrected if I am in error-gave the Canadian Northern in respect to the line between Ottawa and Montreal $6,400 per mile by way of subsidy.
