speechtext:
At all events, the total of the Dominion guarantee here was something like $8,000,000. Then, the Government of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition in respect to the road from Edmonton to Yellowhead gave a subsidy of

$13,000 a mile for fifty miles; $25,000 a mile for one hundred miles; and $35,000 a mile for one hundred and two miles; making the total proceeds about $6,000,000. The Canadian Northern Pacific is the line extending for five hundred and twenty-five miles from the summit of the Rockies to the Pacific coast, and on that, as the right hon. gentleman has pointed out, the Government of British Columbia has given a guarantee at the rate of $35,000 per mile and this Parliament last session gave a subsidy of $12,000 per mile; making a total of $6,000,000 by way of Dominion subsidy to that line.
Prom Ottawa to Toronto, 250 miles, the estimated cost is, I think, about $41,000 per mile, and no guarantee and no subsidy has been given in respect to that line. I desire to point out the difference between the case of the Canadian Northern railway and the older lines which have become entrenched in the Eastern provinces and have acquired rights-of-way and terminals at an early date and at much less expense than the Canadian Northern can. because we all know that the cost of terminals in ereat cities, and the cost of a right-of-way through populous provinces is enormous. We now propose to give a subsidy of $6,400 per mile, which is the ordinary subsidy, on the line running between Ottawa and Toronto. The total guarantees in respect of the lines I have mentioned, namely, the line from Montreal to Port Arthur, the line from Port Arthur to Winnipeg, the line from Winnipeg to Edmonton, the line from Edmonton to the summit of the Rockies, and thence to Vancouver, amount to $57,000,000.
I thought mv hon. friend said $120,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. that is for the whole system. I was careful to say that, as we are giving subsidies on the Transcontinental line, I am now directing the attention of the House particularly to the Transcontinental line, and therefore I am stating that the guarantee given with respect to the line from Montreal to Yellowhead. is $57.000,000, as I have it here, or $50,000,000, as the Minister of Railways has it: but I will be liberal and call it $57,000,000, as I have figured it out at that.
The distance from Montreal, as I have it. to the Yellowhead pass is 2,700 miles, and the guarantee averages $20,000 per mile. I have shown what the guarantee per mile amounted to in the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Let us see now what subsidies have been given to the Canadian Northern in comparison to subsidies given to the Canadian Pacific railway and to the Grand Trunk Pacific in respect of the construction of that line.

Would the minister be good enough to give us a statement of Mr. WHITE (Leeds).
the total amount of guarantee for all purposes to the Canadian Northern, which I understood to be in the vicinity of $122,000.000, in order that we may have the full information as to what governmental assistance or subventions have gone to this whole enterprise? Can he give us the amount of subsidies voted, covering the whole system and the amount actually earned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The subsidies with which
I am dealing now are the subsidies given by the Dominion for the main line.
Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have not spoken at
present about the subsidies given by any province, but I do not believe any province has given anything except the land grant from Selwood to Port Arthur to the Transcontinental line. I shall endeavour to obtain that information a little later on. I think the Minister of Railways has it here.

If my hon. friend desires to give a complete statement of what assistance this country has given to the enterprise, he should give the information as to the amount of the subsidies that have actually been voted or earned covering the whole system.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I propose to give the subsidies at this particular time in respect of the line with which we are dealing, namely, the transcontinental line of the Canadian Northern, because my argument is that the Dominion Government is following out the ordinary policy, and is amply justified in granting these subsidies to the Canadian Northern in respect only of its transcontinental line.

In making the comparison along the lines on which the hon. minister is proceeding, he is not making an argument that is illuminative, because, in dealing with the Canadian Pacific railway, he is dealing with an enterprise that started as a transcontinental line. The Canadian Northern railway has developed its enterprise by successively linking up various local lines in different places. My hon. friend is proposing to carve out of all these lines what he calls a transcontinental railway, and is giving subventions for some of them. He mu'st give the total amount of subventions in addition to the guarantees.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That would be very pertinent to a discussion as to the branch lines in the several provinces. If I had thought my hon. friend would require it, I would have had it here.
My hon. friend is hardly making a fair statement when he says that the Canadian

Pacific railway went on and developed its enterprise. It is true that it did; but, what I dealt with when I was discussing the matter of aid given to the Canadian Pacific railway, was the aid that was given to it in Tespect of its main lines. When I discussed the Grand Trunk Pacific, I discussed and gave figures only in respect of its main line from Winnipeg to Prince Rupert. I did not give any figures as to the Grand Trunk Pacific lines through Saskatchewan and Alberta. I instituted a perfectly fair comparison between the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian Northern main lines.
What was my hon. friend's object in giving the guaranteed subsidies to this line?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There has been a great
deal said along the line that the Canadian Northern has built all its lines with Dominion or provincial help. The reason I put that merged statement on the table was to show not only the character of the enterprise as to vastness and cost, but the amount of money that had been raised by the Canadian Northern Railway Company itself in respect to securities issued by it.
The statement was not complete. In order to have a complete statement, we should have the cash subsidies given to the enterprise everywhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would be true with regard to the system as a whole; it would not interfere with the fact that the Canadian Northern Railway Company had raised $150,000,000 on the strength of its own securities.
That applies to the whole system.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am stating that.
Then why not give the subventions to the whole system ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no reason why I should not do so, if it were pertinent to my argument, but it is not.
The information is inaccurate without it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend the Minister of Railways tells me he will give it in a moment. I do not want the House to get away from the comparison I have instituted between the Canadian Pacific railway, the Grand Trunk Pacific railway and the Canadian Northern railway. I am laying down the principle that private enterprises cannot build transcontinental lines of a national character, having regard to the physical difficulties that they will encounter and the cost of construction in this country unless they receive, as they
have always done, a measure of aid from the Government.

So far so good. We do not dispute that. My hon. friend started to give the House, in order to reply, as he said, to certain surmises or allegations, the whole of the assets which have come to that enterprise. He put down guaranteed subsidies at $120,000,000, unguaranteed subsidies at $145,000,000. His object was to give the whole assets of the company. If he wants to do that, he should also give the cash subsidies which the company had received.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They will have to be tabulated. I think my right hon. friend is making a mountain out of a mole hill.
Sir WILFRID L.AURIER: My hon. friend stated that he would give us the assets of the company. He should give the whole or nothing at all, if he is to make a fair comparison between the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon. friend does not follow me. I am making an argument as to the main line, not on the merged statement. I did not volunteer that information; my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) asked for it, and I gave it in a general way, just as I generally described the Canadian Northern railway, in order that the House might understand what a vast system it was in the matter of transportation in this country. 1 propose to continue the comparison of the line in respect of those portions of the system which are transcontinental in their character.
As I said when I was asked some questions by hon. gentlemen opposite, the total guarantees on 2,700 miles lay the Dominion and the provinces is $20,000 a mile in respect of the transcontinental line from Montreal to Port Arthur, from Port Arthur to Edmonton, from Edmonton to Vancouver, and from Ottawa to Toronto.
We now come to the land grants. It has been suggested that the Canadian Northern railway received vast land grants from the Dominion. As my hon. friend the Minister of Railways has said, they received no land grants direct from the Dominion. In 1897, 1898, and I think in 1899, they purchased the charters of three railways which had obtained, in some oases ten years previously and I think none later than 1890, certain land grants from the Dominion Government in consideration of building those lines. Therefore the Canadian Northern Railway Company received no lands grants itself from the Dominion of Canada.
They bought the charters of lines which had been granted ten years before in some cases, carrying grants of lands in Manitoba from the Dominion Government in

consideration of building their lines. The companies had failed to carry out their enterprises and earn the land grants. The Canadian Northern railway took these over, built the lines and in that way earned the land grants. So it cannot be said that the Canadian Northern railway received any land grant from the Dominion Government. Now, my hon. friend from Welland, (Mr. German) seems quite jocular over it, tout I fancy that if he had bought these railway charters, and had taken over their covenants, he would have thought that he had secured these land grants by purchase and not by grant from the Dominion Government. Once the charter is granted with the land grant attached, it is a question outside of Parliament, and if another railway company or anybody else acquires it and carries out the covenant, the land grants are gained by purchase.

How much
were they?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think about four and a
half million acres. The right hon. gentleman knows all about this matter, because they were dealt with under his regime, and I never heard that he questioned the transactions.
Now we come to the question of subsidy. I desire to make a fair statement on that subject to the House. A subsidy of $12,000 a mile is granted on the line from Ottawa to Port Arthur. No subsidy is granted from Montreal to Ottawa, because, as I pointed out, the Government of my right hon. friend gave a suhsidy with regard to that part of the line. Now, a subsidy of $12,000 a mile is unusually large having regard to what is ordinarily given. But it is not unprecedentedly large, nor do I believe that, having regard to the cost of construction estimated by my hon. friend from South Renfrew on the line between Montreal and Port Arthur, which is $55,000 a mile, it would strike one as an unreasonable subsidy. It is considerably in excess of the $6,400 a mile which is the maximum ordinarily granted, tout it is not larger than has been granted. You have an immense stretch of land along the north shore of Lake Superior, the cost of construction over which will be very great. You have in addition the cost of rights of way in Ontario, and also the cost of terminals. I have gone into this matter in order to inform myself as much as possible, and I find that the cost of terminals for this transcontinental line in the several cities is estimated to be $40,000,000.
What will be the cost of the line from Ottawa to Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not sure. They are building a tunnel at Montreal, but that, no doubt, will be partly paid for by the Mr. WHITE (Leeds).	>
increased valua which the tunnel will give to the lands that they have acquired. But the cost of that does not enter into the present argument. I have said that this subsidy of $12,000 a mile is not unprecedented. If my memory serves_ me correctly, the Government of my right hon. friend gave a subsidy of $11,000 a mile in respect of a line from Lethbridge through the Crow's Nest pass to Nelson. Last session we gave a subsidy of $12,000 a mile on a more expensive construction through British Columbia. I think that the Canadian Central, between Pembroke and Callender, received $12,000 a mile. According to our ordinary way of doing things, if a line is built costing over $25,000 a mile, a subsidy of $6,400 is given-which is about twenty-five per cent. In connection with a line costing $18,000 the subsidy is $2,300-my hon. friend from South Renfrew will correct me if I am wrong. So, it would appear that from twenty to twenty-five per cent is given as subsidy in respect of lines as ordinarily built. But the phenomena of recent times so far as Tailway construction is concerned have been the enormous cost of building through the old settled parts of Canada, owing to the increased cost of rights of way and of terminals. As we all know, land in Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver, Victoria and other places, has doubled, trebled, quadrupled in some cases, in the last five or ten years. We know the enormous cost of acquiring terminals in these cities. Therefore, a subsidy in excess of $6,400 a mile is not unreasonable for a transcontinental line. 1 have a statement here of the total subsidies received in respect of the main line of the Canadian "Northern railway from Quebec to Vancouver. It shows total subsidies of $8,000,000, of which $5,000,000 has been received. Now, I ask hon. members to compare this with the figures I gave. And let it be remembered that this includes $6,000,000 from Summit down. The Canadian Northern railway, in respect of its lines east of the Rocky mountains, has received almost nothing by way of subsidies on the main line, and it is the main line I am dealing with, because it is to the main line that we are giving these subsidies. No subsidy has been given from Ottawa to Port Arthur; none from Ottawa to Toronto; none from Winnipeg to Edmonton; none from Edmonton to Summit. And no subsidy has been given this line from Port Arthur to Winnipeg, except a small amount in respect of the line from Port Arthur to Rainy River.

The hon.
minister says that the line from Quebec to Summit has received only $8,000,000 of subsidy, and has stated the portions of

road over which subsidies have not been given. Will he state the portions of the road that have been subsidized to the amount of $8,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: From Ottawa to Hawkesbury, a subsidy of $367,000. My hon. friend has asked me for a statement of the portions of the lines that have not previously been subsidized. I will take them up alternately. Ottawa to Port Arthur, 900 miles, no subsidy. It is in respect of those portions of the line to which no subsidies have previously been applied that we are now giving subsidies. Stanley to Fort Frances, subsidies granted, $1,355,000. Stanley is a short distance outside of Port Arthur. Fort Frances to Rainy River, subsidies of $179,000. Winnipeg to Yellowhead, no subsidies.

There are the
4,000,000 acres of land.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The 4,000.000 acres of land were acquired from the Winnipeg and Hudson Bay Railway Company, the Lake Manitoba Railway and Canal Company, and the Manitoba and Southeastern Railwav Company. The Canadian Northern Railway Company purchased those lands, fust as my right hon. friend might have done himself.
The last sum mentioned is for that portion of the road from Winnipeg southerly to the lake of the Woods.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no doubt mv hon. friend is right; at all events I am dealing now with cash subsidies in the ordinary sense. Subsidies in respect of the line from Y-ellowhead pass to Vancouver were granted at the last session of Parliament to the amount of $6,186,000. These amounts, together with a small subsidy in respect of the line between Montreal and Quebec, make up the $8,000,000 which I have mentioned as being the total amount of cash subsidies paid in respect of the Transcontinental line from Quebec to Vancouver.
Mv impression was that the subsidy from Quebec to Montreal was a very generous one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: $1,194,000. We are considering resolutions to-day under which the Government proposes to grant subsidies in respect of sections of the Transcontinental line of the Canadian Northern with reeard to which no subsidies have up to date been granted. From Ottawa to Port Arthur, no subsidies were granted; Edmonton to Summit, no subsidies; Toronto to Ottawa, no subsidies; Winnipeg to Port Arthur, subsidies to the amount of $1,500,000.

Does the minister
put any valuation on the 4,000,000 acres of land?
Only 1,250,000 acres of land apply to the main line.

The minister spoke about 4,000,000 acres of land, and I understood him to decline when the hon. leader of the Opposition asked him to speak about that in connection with the argument he was making. The Minister of Railways said that a million and a Quarter acres of that
4,000,000 should be allotted to the main line. What valuation does the minister put on the 4,000,000 acres?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think I can give my
hon. friend some information with regard to that, but it may not be as definite as he desires. As I have pointed out, the Canadian Northern Railway Company acquired from these three lines in Manitoba the land grants to which they were entitled upon carrying out their undertakings with the Government in respect of the construction of their lines. ^ In 1898, 1899 and 1900 the price of land in the West was very different from what it is to-day. I will give my hon. friend an experience I had that will, I think, be very ilhiminating to him with regard to these very lands which he has in mind. In 1899 the Canadian Northern Railway Company made what was called a land grant bond issue; they issued bonds to expend $2,000,000 secured upon 1,365,000 acres of land. That is at the rate of $1.50 an acre, supposed to .represent fifty per cent of the value of these lands. Sales were made at $4, $5, and $6 an acre of the substantial portion of that 1,365,000 acres, and the balance of the 4,000,000 acres to which I have referred, and which was acquired from the railway .companies I have mentioned, was sold at $8, $9, $10, and probably is now selling at $15 an acre. It is therefore impossible for me to state with any great accuracy what these lands are worth, because some of them have not yet been sold. I believe ithat the comparatively .small amount sold last year realized something like $15 an acre. The hon. member for Calgary, who I have no doubt is well informed, tells me that at the time of the sale the lands were worth about $4 an acre. I know however that for the purposes of this land grant mortgage, $3 an acre was estimated to be their value, and the land grant mortgage made by the Canadian Northern and secured by this 1,365,000 acres of land was on the basis of about $1.50 an acre, representing fifty per cent of their estimated value at that time. They call them prairie lands.

How long ago was
that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It was in 1899. A railway company, generally speaking, must sell; they are not like the ordinary holder of land, because the object of the railway company is to get the land settled in order to obtain the traffic. Their efforts are directed



at colonization, and we know the success that has attended the great work done by the Canadian Northern railway in connection with the colonization of the Saskatchewan valley and the West generally.
Now, I come to a particular transaction that seems unusual, but I think it marks a very forward advance in connection with the granting of subsidies of this kind. I say frankly that the amount granted on account of tfhe large cost of construction, the increase in the cost of labour, and material, $12,000 a mile was large as compared with the usual and ordinary subsidy of $6,400 a mile. The Government, having regard to the cost of these lines and to the large sums of money that have still to be raised by the railway company in order that the entire transcontinental line may be ultimately built, as shown by the figures submitted by the Minister of Railways, felt justified in granting favourable consideration to the application of the Canadian Northern railway in respect to the subsidies, which are confined, as I have said, to the main line, and do not extend to the lines in the several provinces. But as it was unusual in amount and distinguishable even from the subsidy which last year was given in respect of the line between Summit and Vancouver, running through the Rocky mountains, and costing $70,000 or $80,000 a mile as compared with $50,000 or $55,000 estimated by the hon. member for South Renfrew in respect of the line between Ottawa and Port Arthur the Government took the position that they should receive some consideration of a substantial character from the Canadian Northern Railway Company. I shall point out to the House that in conection with these subsidies., legislation was introduced some time ago or the provision embodied in subsidy bills, I am not quite sure which, under which three per cent upon the amount of subsidy given to a railway is deducted from the amount earned by the railways for the carrying, of the mails. Therefore, when subsidies are given to railway companies, the Dominion Government, while giving the subsidy, on the other hand receive back three per cent on that amount, this sum being deducted from the amount earned by the railway company in respect of the carriage of mail. That is embodied in this Bill to the extent of the $6,400 per mile which is the usual and ordinary subsidy. I desire to point out in this connection that the Canadian Northern railway is at a disadvantage in comparison with other transcontinental lines with which it is in competition and which had constructed their lines of railways and received subsidies prior to the time when this policy was put into effect and therefore I think it is reasonable that the three per cent should Mr. WHITE (Leeds).	,
be charged only on the $6,400 a mile, especially in view of the consideration which we are receiving from the Canadian Northern and which, in my judgment, marks a distinct advance upon the policy hitherto adopted in regard to subsidizing these roads. The Government said: As a consideration from the Canadian Northern Railway Company, having regard to these subsidies, justifiable as we believe in themselves but exceeding the amount usually granted, we desire to obtain a certain portion of the common stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. That appeals to me as advanced and sound legislation. If the Governor in Council had received a block of stock of the Canadian Pacific railway in the earlier days it would have been a most valuable asset to the Dominion to-day and therefore it seems to me to be proper and good policy that, as we gave a large subsidy to the Canadian Northern railway, we should receive from the Canadian Northern railway a block' of their common stock so that in the event of that Tailway succeeding as the Canadian Pacific railway succeeded or even in less measure-and I am sure everyone hopes it will succeed-then the Dominion of Canada will have a valuable asset in the stock of that, road. We have obtained from the Canadian Northern Railway Company, 70,000 shares of the par value of $7,000,000 of the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. The question naturally arises, what is the value of that stock? The Minister of Railways has indicated that it is of indeterminate value. At the same time, it has been, deemed of very considerable value. Personally, I have known of transactions, few in number, in excess of forty dollars a share. I find by their statement of earnings that the balance of the credit of income account in the statement as of June 30, 1912, is about $6,000,000. That is the accumulated profit since the road has been in operation. I may say that there is $25,000,000 of common stock of the $70,000,000 issued by the Canadian Northern railway that is held in trust to be availed of, if they so elect, by the holders of the income charge convertible debenture stock outstanding. In other words, the holders of that stock have the right to take at par this $25,000,000 of Canadian Northern railway stock. The stock we are taking is the stock of the parent organization, that is, of the company which controls 4.500 miles o.f road in the Northwest from Port Arthur to Edmonton.

Is this $25,000,000-
which was reserved to meet the convertible bonds in addition to the $70,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The $70,000,000 is the entire authorized issue, and if the holders of the income convertible stock elect to take a like amount at par of the Canadian

Northern stock them, to that extent, the $25,000,000 shares will be in the hands of people who have paid $100 a share for them or who may be the holders of income convertible debenture stock.

And the Government
will be the owners of practically one-sixth of the stock.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yets. Therefore, taking
the whole capital stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, which controls 4,500 miles in the West, and owning, I believe, the Canadian Northern Quebec system, and affiliated with the other systems with the ultimate idea of amalgamating them all into a system extending over the continent, the Dominion owns one-tenth of that stock.

The $25,000,000 is held
by the Canadian Northern railway; it has not been issued to anyone?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is in trust.
Has the balance of the $70,000,000 been issued?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am unable to say, but I believe the balance of the issue has been issued, it is reported as issued.
And for what consideration and to whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am unable to say. I shall deal with that in a few moments. The general report is that the balance of the stock of the Canadian Northern railway has been issued to the contracting firm of Mackenzie and Mann and Company in consideration of their agreeing to build the line for that and other considerations, and I suppose for financing the enterprise to its present degree.
The contracting firm have been paid in cash for building the line.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend will be patient I will come to that, and I think I can explain it in a manner that will be satisfactory to my hon. friend.

If it is satisfactory to
my hon. friend it will be satisfactory to me.
How did the number of shares come to be fixed at 70,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
By legislation of this Parliament. The $70,000,000 is the authorized stock of the parent company under legislation of this Parliament, one-tenth of which the Government acquires in consideration of a subsidy which is above the ordinary, but which, I believe, is justifiable, having	regard	to the factsI have laid	before	the House.
That is the position. I have no hesita-
370i
tion in saying that in the case of subsidies of such a character given to railways, and, I believe, necessarily, in order that they nay complete their line, it is only proper that the Government should take the step of saying we desire some consideration from you other than the consideration mentioned in the ordinary subsidy bill. Might I say that the Canadian Northern Ontario owns the securities of various subsidiary companies. I find in its annual statement a list of acquired securities of a very important character. There is the Minnesota and Ontario Bridge Company, the debenture stock and bonds of which it owns; the Minnesota and Manitoba railway, which had to be a separate line in Minnesota and the bonds and stock of which it owns; the Lake Superior Terminals Company, which has the elevators at Port Arthur, and the bonds and stock of which are owned by the Canadian Northern railway; the Canadian Northern Telegraph Company, the mortgage bonds and capital stock of which are owned by the Canadian Northern railway; the Winnipeg Land Company, limited, the Canadian Northern Coal and Ore Dock Company, the St. Boniface and Western Land Company, the Edmonton and Slave Lake Railway Company, whose line runs from Edmonton to Athabaska Landing, and whose first mortgage bonds and stock are owned by the Canadian Northern railway; the Canadian Northern Prairie Lands Company,, the capital stock of which is owned by" the Canadian Northern railway, the Canadian Northern Railway Express Company, limited, the first mortgage bonds and capital stock of which are owned by the Canadian Northern railway; and the Canadian Northern Steamships, limited, the debenture stock and capital stock of which are owned by the Canadian Northern railway. That is the company which runs the Royal George and Royal Edward between Montreal and Bristol.
Do they own any of the bonds or stock of the Canadian Northern Alberta Company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think I can make this general statement-I tried to go into this matter fairly as Finance Minister. The Canadian Northern, as the parent company, owns I think the stock of the Canadian Northern Quebec, and I believe the Canadian Northern has guaranteed the debenture stock of that line. But part of the stock of the Canadian Northern Quebec is owned by the former holders of the stock of the Great Northern Railway Company, which was taken over by the Canadian Northern Quebec. The Canadian Northern Ontario, the parent company, does not own as yet the stock of the Canadian Northern Alberta Company; only

$250,000 of that stock has been issued, I think.

Has the Canadian
Northern Alberta a provincial charter?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think it has a Dominion charter; at any rate, it is under Dominion jurisdiction, because the Government of my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) guaranteed its bonds, and we extended 'the guarantee last year. I have dealt in a very general way, and I hope not in a tedious manner, -with a rather complicated question. The transaction that we propose is one of magnitude. The subsidies are large, but having regard to the transportation problems which confront this country, and having regard to the policy which prevailed in the past in respect to the Canadian Pacific railway and in more recent years in respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific, I think that the Government has only aided to a fair and reasonable extent the construction of the transcontinental section of the Canadian Northern railway which plays such a part in the transportation problems of Canada to-day, and which is such a vast and costly enterprise.
My hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German) is looking at me wistfully or curiously. He has probably in mind the question which he put to me a little while ago. Let me make a sort of public confession of faith with regard to the question of the capitalization of railways. I am not going to criticise my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and his Government. There is progress in this matter. There is progress in the United States as well as in Canada; but if I had any criticism to make of legislation in recent years in the United States or in Canada, with respect to the capitalization of railway companies, it would be this, that sufficient care is not taken to see that the capitalization is not an unduly large amount.
Hear, hear

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Parliament and parliamentary committees are at a disadvantage in fixing the amount of the capitalization of a railway company. Too often legislation is put through authorizing bonding powers to the extent say of $30,000 or $40,000 a mile, and authorizing a large amount of capital stock, say of $10,000,000 or $20,000,000 without consideration or criticism. A portion of that stock may find its way into the hands of holders all over the world, and in time dividends are paid at 100 cents in the dollar. As I say, sufficient care is not exercised, and can hardly be exercised by Parliament in that regard. I look forward to the time when the Railway Commission would be charged with the duty of saying whether the canitalization of a railway comnanv was fair, and whether a certain Mr. WHITE (Leeds)
stock issue should be made. I am only giving or indicating my own views. My hon. friend (Mr. German) says that the stock of the Canadian Northern railway has not been paid up in cash. Possibly in part it may have been issued for services rendered in construction and otherwise in bringing the railway to its present condition of construction. It is, I believe, an undoubted fact in connection with that company that a considerable portion of the stock issued has not been paid full in cash. What has been done is done, so far as legislation is concerned. The Government of my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has given to the Canadian Northern Ontario and to the other roads their charter powers so far as the issue of bonds and of stock is concerned. So far as our action with regard to this railway is concerned, I desire to make the general statement, which I have emphasized throughout my argument, that, having regard to the necessity, if Confedration is to hold together, for transportation facilities, and in accordance with the policy that Canada shall have abundant facilities and complete channels of communication between east and west for the movement of her crops and merchandise, the Government feels that it is abundantly justified, on the facts and information which I have presented to the House, in granting to the Canadian Northern Railway company the subsidies referred to in this resolution. That enterprise is one of great importance, one of the greatest in Canada.
I think I have given to the House full information as to that. It has been prosecuted with great enterprise and even daring by those who have been associated with it. It appeared to the Government, and I make the statement without any hesitation, that the aid now asked by way of subsidy is not unreasonable or out of accord with the policy pursued in days past with regard to the Canadian Pacific railway, and, in more recent years, with respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific. Under the circumstances, therefore, I think that the subsidies are justified. The Government has made a greater forward advance upon any policy in the past by reason of the fact that it has acquired, in respect of the larger subsidies, seventy thousand shares or one-tenth of the capital stock of the Canadian Northern Railway company.

My hon. friend says that $25,000,000 worth of the stock is held by the Canadian Northern in trust and $45,000,000, the balance of the stock, has been issued to Mackenzie & Mann or the contracting company. Out of which stock does the $7,000,000 come?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The $7,000,000 could not

come out of the $25,000,000, because that is held in trust.

If Mackenzie & Mann
have earned $45,000,000, why give them $7,000,000 ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am isure my hon. friend does not want to put words in my mouth that I did not use; I am not in a position to state that the balance of the stock has gone to Mackenzie & Mann. The stock is not listed in any exchange; there are very few holders of it, and its value at present is indeterminate. Whether the stock is valuable or not, and I think it is of considerable value, the Government has obtained one-tenth of the stock, and the $25,000,000 held in trust can only be devoted to the purposes of the trust. Let me put it this way: a railway company issues debenture stock which is different in character from capital stock, because it is an obligation of the company, and the purchasers of debenture stock are given a right within a certain number of years to surrender that stock for which they have paid the market value.
Some of it sold as high as one hundred and six.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The privilege is given the holders of that debenture stock to exchange for the capital stock up to 1916, the amount of debentures they had acquired. Therefore, $25,000,000 of the $70,000,000 is fixed with that trust, and it must be devoted to the purpose for which it was placed in trust.
Suppose it is not called on, what becomes of it ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is in the treasury of the company. I am not in a position to say whether the balance of the stock has been issued to Mackenzie & Mann or mot. My view would be that if they are the contractors, it probably has been issued to them; but I draw no conclusion from that except that probably it was not paid in full in cash. That is to say, a certain proportion may have been paid by reason of the services rendered, but how much I am unable to say. The point I am making is, that the legislation under which the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company was fixed at $70,000,000, is the legislation of this Parliament, and the contracts under which that stock has been issued, are contracts which I have no doubt are valid under the law of the province in which they were made. It is open, of course, to say that it is unwise policy on the part of the Government to overcapitalize railway companies, and that regard should be had to the cost of the road. I concur in that view of my hon. 'riend (Mr. German); but I do not think
it touches the question I have been dealing with as to whether or not it is proper to extend this aid to the Canadian Northern Railway Company. By way of analogy, let me ask my hon. friend if he knows where the stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific company is ?
I suppose it is held by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, because they guaranteed the whole enterprise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: What has become of the stock of the Canadian Northern Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I inquired as to that, and I do not believe it is issued. I am told that only $250,000 of it is issued. The cases are not analogous; the Canadian Northern has not guaranteed the securities of the Canadian Northern Ontario; they have financed with provincial Government guarantees, and in addition to that they have made a debenture stock issue of their own, not guaranteed by any railway company. So that, the parent company has not guaranteed the debenture stock of the

Canadian Northern Ontario Company, and I am told that only $250,000 of that stock is issued. When my hon. friend comes to deal with that, he will probably advert to the fact that the late Government granted the Canadian Northern Ontario its stockissuing power, and he will no doubt be able to tell us the amount of that stock, and why they were given power to issue stock to the amount of capitalization which they possessed.	*
I have made a longer speech than I intended, but my sole desire was to place before parliament and the country the information I have been able to acquire, in pursuance of my duties as Minister of Finance in connection with this transaction. In view of the information I have placed before the House, and the argument with which I have endeavoured to support it, I feel that the House and the country will say that the subsidies given to the Canadian Northern are fair and reasonable, having regard to the enterprise they have undertaken and in comparison with the aid offered to other transcontinental lines, and in strict accordance with the policy which has prevailed in recent years, and which is still necessary if we are to solve to the satisfaction of the people of Canada the transportation problems which confront us.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM: I have not a great deal of fault to find with my hon. friend's figures, except that they were very intricate, and probably that may have been necessary. It would be difficult for a member of parliament or for an elector to follow these various meanderings of the different companies, and the different guarantees, and the different subsidies, and the different names, and the different uses to which subsidies have been put. The question of transportation is a big one for Canada yet. I understood the argument of the Minister of Finance, outside of his statement, largely to be on behalf of doing something for the Canadian Northern enterprise. I want to say Tight here that I take no issue with him on that. The people of Canada did a great deal for the first transcontinental railway, and I am not going to enter into any comparisons now. My own opinion is that comparisons have Very little to do with the question before us, which is a concrete one and does not require to be discussed at length. As to whether or not we did a great deal for the Canadian Pacific railway, there is a difference of opinion. Looking at it from this distance and from the history of the country, I think, if it did require some sacrifice, it has been worth it to the country; and Canada is now the home of the greatest transportation system in the) Mr. WHITE ((Leeds).
known world. It is a well managed system. Conditions then were so altogether different from conditions now, that to attempt a comparison would not be of much value.
A great deal has been said about the Grand Trunk Pacific, and I will not stop to discuss it in detail. My hon. friend the hon. Minister of Finance answered himself in regard to guarantees and said, what is true, that Canada does not expect to be called upon to pay any money on these guarantees. Notwithstanding the figures placed before the House, this much must be borne in mind in reference to that enterprise, that when it is completed and all the cost is counted, be it greater or less than anticipated, Canada will own 1802 miles of the highest standard of railway on the continent of America. Although it is leased to a company, the title to 1802 miles rests in the name of the people of Canada and will be a big lever in time to come in governing what shall be done in regard to transportation in this country.
Let us come down to the present. The Canadian Northern railway interests are divided into so many different branches that I am not surprised that my hon. friend has found difficulty in chasing them all up. I am afraid he missed a few. Some came into my mind that he did not mention. In the first place, we have Mackenzie & Mann who are the foundation, the beginning and the end of all these enterprises. We have the Canadian Northern Alberta, the Canadian Northern Pacific, the Canadian Northern Ontario, the Canadian Northern Quebec; we have at least a dozen other lines under different names that have been acquired by these interests. It is such an intricate matter that to discuss it even before such a well informed body as Parliament, would-not be attempted by me for a moment. It is also a difficult matter if we deal with it as a matter of stocks, bonds and securities. I shall dismiss all that in a word. So far as I am concerned, and I believe all hon. members, we are prepared to do something for the Canadian Northern system at the present time. What is it to be; how are we to do it, and what are we to get for doing it?
My hon. friend mentioned a subsidy of $11,000 a mile to the Crowsnest Pass railway. It will be remembered by those who were in the House at that time that, when the Government did that, they secured from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company a most favourable concession as regards freight rates, and in other ways, such as coal areas. I am not saying what ought to be asked from the Canadian Northern Railway Company at the present moment. When any company comes asking favours, it is a good time to ask something in return for the benefit of the people of Canada. The Canadian Northern Ontario system

received from this Government a guarantee of $35,000 a mile from Montreal to Port Arthur. That approximated $35,000,000. Less than that was realized on the sale of the bonds. The Premier rather criticised me on that occasion for giving the cost of the road at the figure I mentioned. I attempted to justify the guarantee of $35,000 a mile by the statement that the road, if properly constructed, would cost in the vicinity of $50,000 a mile. I think equipment was included in that. These figures are justified to-day by the present Government. No road of modern construction in that territory can be built for a less sum of money. It was wise to place in that contract a clause outlining or defining, approximately at least, a standard to which the road should attain before they got this amount of money.
There are two ways of aiding roads. One is by .subsidies and the other by guarantees. The Canadian Northern usually asks a guarantee from the Dominion Government and a subsidy from the provincial .authorities. In many oases in the West they have got a guarantee from the provincial authorities and a subsidy from the Dominion Government. It is not often that a company asks for a subsidy and a guarantee from the same source. I am not going to quarrel with the request because I am not altogether acquainted with the reasons for it. The Minister of Railways has given us some particulars or rather comparisons with other roads. _ I do not think the comparison is a striking one and it does not enter into the calculation at all. Does the Canadian Northern require aid in order to complete its transcontinental line? If it does, we would have to consider very seriously before we would decline to give aid in some way under such conditions. Why? The Government of this country, whether it is this Government or the preceding one, has linked its name with this transcontinental line, and the credit of Canada as well is linked with this transcontinental line as it is linked with other transcontinental lines. In dealing with it from that point of view I think a certain amount of care is necessary, and the Dominion of Canada cannot afford to let the Canadian Northern enterprise collapse or do anything like collapsing. I am not saying that it is in such a condition at all. I do not wish to leave that inference. This is a great enterprise and no person can accuse me of having any antipathy against it, because during my term of office I took so much interest in it that some of the other roads thought I was going too far. I always claimed I was doing the best I could for the people of Canada, whether it was the Canadian Pacific, the Grand Trunk Pacific, or the Canadian Northern.
I hold strong views .as to what governments ought to do, not for railway companies but for the people who use railways. It has been said-and it is a good demagogic argument-that we must not do anything for railways. I hold no brief for the companies; but we must bear in mind that every dollar that Canada has spent in aiding railway companies has been for the purpose of enabling the man who works on the farm or in the shop to get a bigger return for his daily labour, by carrying his products to and from market at a oheaper rate and with fair speed. That is the principle underlying aid to railways and other transportation organizations. We want to adhere to that .principal. That is the reason I do not object at alii to doing something for the Candian Northern railway. It may be a question of how we will do it, or what we will do. I go further perhaps than some other hon. gentlemen would go. Living in the old part of Canada, where we have railway facilities, where we can get on a train when we please, having a choice of trains every day to go where we like, we are apt to think it is time we should cease giving assistance to these transportation companies, forgetting that we have brought men to Canada, forgetting that we have brought women to Canada, wbo live in places ten, twenty, forty, fifty, a hundred miles from a railway. I say it is the duty of the people, of Canada, enjoying the privileges we do, to continue lending our assistance until all the places to which we bring people to help to build up Canada have railway facilities approximately as good as those we have in the older part of the country. That is the only way in which we can make the people of Canada contented, prosperous and happy.
Well what are we to do for the Canadian Northern railway? In the first place, now is the time when, if we have any little grievance which the Parliament of Canada should straighten out with either the Canadian Northern railway or the Grand Trunk Pacific, that grievance should be remedied. I have a grievance against the Canadian Northern Railway system-and against the Government, too, though I think perhaps the Government did not understand thoroughly what they were doing. Last year this Government by statute exempted five hundred miles of the Canadian Northern railway transcontinental line from the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners of Canada-not the Canadian Northern railway, but as stated in the statute, the Canadian Northern Pacific, from the Rocky mountains pass down to Vancouver. The Canadian Northern Pacific last year was given $12,000 a mile-about $6,000,000, as a subsidy. But the provision that is put in every other subsidy agreement that the rates of the railway sub-

sidized shall be under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners, was left out in this case. So we are in the position to-day of being asked for further aid to a line on which the Board of Railway Commissioners cannot control the rates.-and that, a transcontinental line from Montreal to Vancouver.

May I ask a question? I am sure the hon. member would not willingly leave a false impression. The provincial Act incorporating this line contained express provision that it should not be subject to the Board of Railway Commissioners, but that the rates should be fixed by the Lieut-Governor in Council and this Parliament should have no power to take from the provincial Government, which had incorporated the company the power which that legislation had given. Is not that correct?

It may be. But then
this Government had not any right to give $6,000,000 to a road so restricted, The Canadian Northern railway built the road under a provincial charter in order to get rid of the Board of Railway Commissioners and for other reasons.
They could not have built in any other way.

Yes, they could; they could have come here and got a Dominion charter. The question is simply whether this Government shall control a transcontinental line, or leave a part of that line under control of a provincial government. I have this grievance against the Canadian Northern railway and the Government, and that may crystallize in the form of a resolution before this is through. It is in abrogation of the principle we have adopted in relation to railway affairs. We have a Board of Railway Commissioners, part of whose duty is to control rates; and in every subsidy Act for many years has been inserted the clause under which a provincial road accepting a subsidy from this Parliament shall be subject to the Board of Railway Commissioners. But this road was excepted. If it had been only a provincial road, with provincial objects alone, there might have been a reason for this, or there might be excuse, at least. But this is part of a transcontinental line. To-day we are asked to give a subsidy to another link in that line; and I say that now is the time to say to the Canadian Northern railway: You must make arrangements, before we give you aid, by which this transcontinental line, every foot of it, shall come under the Railway Commissioners, so that the people may get the benefit of the rates.

Their rates must be under the commission.
Mr. GRAHAM.
They are not, and they need not be.
Yes, must be.

As the Minister of Finance would say, I know what is in the hon. gentleman's mind. He would tell us that under the Act, when this becomes part of a transcontinental line, it comes under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners. That statement was made last year; but the Prime Minister will tell the hon. gentleman that it is not correct. I hate to put my law against that of a learned counsel, but if the hon. gentleman will look at the decision of the Privy Council-
In the Montreal Street railway case, I suppose.

-as to the jurisdiction of the Dominion Board of Railway Com-misioners to control rates, over a partly provincial and partly Dominion road, he will find that the Privv Council has settled it that the Board of Railway Commissioners has no right to control that part of the rate which is made up on the provincially chartered road, and as to the Dominion Railway Act regarding such matters, that Act is ultra vires. This is a provincial road, with a provincial charter. Last year, when this became part of a through line under our Act, some hon. gentlemen said that the rates could be controlled. Now it transpires, by judgment of the Privy Council, that these rates connot be controlled when a provincial road forms part of a through line. That is one of the things I ask the Canadian Northern railway to straighten out before they get this subsidy. For, as the Minister of Finance has pointed out, this is not a provincial road, but is to carry a share of the immense traffic flowing between the East and the West. Every one of the provinces of the Dominion is interested in that section of five hundred miles so far as the traffic east and west is concerned; and. in the interest of all the provinces no part of that road should be exempted from the jurisdiction of the Railway Commissioners.

I think mv
hon. friend will at once see that the Board of Railway Commissioners would fix the rates of traffic from Montreal to Vancouver.

I do not think thev
could.

I submit that they must. The province of British Columbia, over whose Act in this matter we have no control, for some reason best known to itself, has said that the board shall not fix rates from Summit to the coast. But, notwithstanding that, and notwithstanding the de-

cision which I have very carefully considered, the Board of Railway Commissioners would fix the rates from Ottawa to Vancouver. For fifteen hundred miles of that transit would be on roads subiect to the control of the board, and the narticular proportion of a through rate of any portion of the road they would not be able to determine. Do I make myself clear?
I am not auite sure that I catch the drift of that argument.

If the question were at issue before the Board of Railway Commissioners as to a through rate from Ottawa to Vancouver over the Canadian Northern railway, that tribunal would have the jurisdiction. In any event, it is conceded that it has complete and supreme control up to Summit. From Summit to the coast the province of British Columbia has said that the Lieutenant Governor in Council will assert supreme control, but with regard to the fixing of the through rates from Ottawa to Vancouver, surely if the Board of Railway Commissioners exercises the control which is given to it over the 1,500 miles of transit, it will only be a matter of deciding what the 'through rate shall be.

That would be a question as between the railway companies, which the Board of Railway Commissioners would not have power to settle, because they cannot do anything with the provincial line. The company has said to the British Columbia Government that no appeal will 'be made to the Board of Railway Commissioners and should anybody have the temerity to make such an appeal, they are ready to fight it. So the Board of Railway Commissioners so far as a through rate is concerned are absolutely debarred. The British Columbia contracts so provides in order vto control traffic emanating in British Columbia and going outside, as well as traffic emanating outside of British Columbia and coming in, so it is a wider contract than one having application only to the province of British Columbia. In rendering aid to the Canadian Northern Railway Company one of the things that ought 'to be done is put the whole line under the Board of Railway Commissioners.
Notwithstanding the fact that the people of British Columbia say no.

We are legislating for
the Dominion of Canada. If the railway company has placed itself in a peculiar position, it is its business to get out of it. I believe that the proper way to have aided the Canadian Northern Railway Company at the present time would have been by way of loan. It will be in the minds of some persons that if a loan were secured, it would hamper the company in its further
financing if the Dominion of Canada held the securities of the enterprise. It would do this only if the amount were too small to complete the enterprise. I would be prepared if necessary to give twice the amount that is set out in these resolutions and make it a loan so that there would be a sufficient amount of money loaned to the company on a businesslike basis. As to the $7,000,000, I am not going to discuss that. It is possible that the stock may be very valuable, and it may not. I would not say for a moment that it is not of considerable value now, but it is problematical what the future value will be. Will the Government in 'becoming a large stockholder ask for representation on the board of the railway? The Government of Canada now has a representative on the Grand Trunk Pacific Board. I am not going to discuss the extent of his usefulness, but the Government of Canada at the present time is a bondholder of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, and in the Canadian Northern it is going to become a stockholder, holding one-tenth of the entire capital stock of the enterprise. Under these circumstances it strikes me that the Government should ask for representation on the board. If it does, and I think it should, it will become a part owner of the Canadian Northern system, and, whatever its future condition may be, the Government will be bound to see it through. I am a friend of the enterprise; I believe Canada must see it through, but, as I say, I believe aid ought to be given by way of a loan, even if the amount be twice as large, and I think we should not give this money to the Canadian Northern until they place their entire line under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners.
