House again in Committee on Bill No. 233, for the relief of Frank William Meek.- Mr. Pardee. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair).

I feel that I cannot allow this Bill to pass through the House without raising my voice in protest against it. I do not feel that it is necessary, even at this late time of the session when we are all anxious to hurry on the work, to apologize for delaying the business of the House for a few moments while I give expression to my views on this Bill. We are recognizing more and more in this country the

value of social questions. We recognize in this land, what is recognized in many other countries, the great evil following the granting of divorces too easily. Divorce is recognized as one of the evils which the great country to the south of us must deal with at no very distant date. We in this country have been very fortunate in the past in the matter of granting divorces, and it is only in the last year or two that applications have come to our Parliament in very great numbers. Now is the time, however, for this Parliament to exercise that care which will prevent the coming, in this land, of an epidemic, so to speak, of that evil which is so prevalent in the land to the south. Divorce is a social question, and it is one which involves the happiness and morality of society. If divorces are improperly granted, attacks are then made on that foundation on which the social structure of our land is reared. It becomes, therefore, most important that this Parliament, which is entrusted with the granting of divorces, should exercise the greatest care in dealing with every such application that comes before this House. I do not wish to take up the time of the House at the present moment to discuss the procedure that is followed in this country in the matter of granting divorce. I do wish, however, to say that while we may object to some of the Bills which have been put through by the Senate committee, we cannot do otherwise than testify to the great patience and care and thought and attention which is devoted to the applications by that committee and especially by its chairman. But even the Senate Committee on Divorce is not infallible. They make mistakes and, in my opinion, when this Bill which is now before us was passed by that committee, they [DOT]made an error. In my mind the decision they arrived at to grant a divorce to the petitioner in this case was not warranted by the evidence. I shall not enter into details of that evidence, but I shall very briefly make a statement of it. The petitioner and the respondent in this case lived together for eighteen years, and, on the testimonv of the petitioner, they had no trouble during all that time. At the end of eighteen years, the respondent decides to leave her husband, according to his story. She, after a few months separation from him, goes to live in another house, an eight-roomed house, in which the only occupants were she and a man. She does not do this secretly; she does not hesitate to let her husband know where she is; she changes the telephone from the house which she and her husband had occupied, to the house where she is now living. Letters of her husband which come to her, she readdresses in her own hand and forwards to him at his address. So that there is Mr. STEELE.
no effort on her part to hide or to_ live secretly. While she spends a year living in this house, a neighbour girl gives evidence that she visited the house almost every day during that time, and she saw nothing improper whatever in the relations between the respondent and the corespondent. Detectives are put on the track, and we all know that the evidence of these men is, perhaps, not the best; but the most that they can testify to in this case is that they saw shadows on the window blinds of the front room of the house, and one was under the impression that there were two people in the room, and that they were in the act of undressing. This is practically the evidence.
Who was the householder ?

There is no evidence given as to who was the householder. The evidence is not very plain on several points which it seems to me it would be most important for this Parliament to have full information upon. Practically all that has been proven is that she left her husband and went and lived in a house, occupying that house with a man for the term of about a year. This may arouse our suspicions, and there may be certain other facts connected with the case which intensify those suspicions. But let me say that there are hundreds of women in this land who, on account of the conduct of their husbands, would feel a great relief in being enabled to leave them and go and earn their living at any occupation for wnich they were adapted. If a woman has no profession or trade, what can she earn that living at ? Nothing else than domestic service, or keeping house for a man. I think this Parliament should hesitate before establishing the precedent that a divorce will be granted to any man whose wife leaves him and goes and lives in a house with another man for a period of some months. I think we should hesitate before stamping any woman who does that as an immoral woman. I think there is a great principle at stake here-that we ought not to pass this Bill until we have further evidence to absolutely corroborate what has been given or to absolutely prove that this woman led a life of immorality after she parted from her husband. For the reasons I have given, I believe that the evidence in this case does not warrant divorce being granted, and does not warrant the House of Commons giving this Bill a third reading.

I quite agree with my
hon. friend from Perth as to the necessity of great care being exercised by this Parliament in the granting of divorce. I confess that of the thirty odd divorce cases which have been considered by the Private

Bills Committee this session, with respect to at least three of them I entertained great doubt as to whether a divorce should be granted. However, with respect to the present case, the evidence which was given, and which was considered very carefully, I think, by the Private Bills Committee, convinced me absolutely that the respondent was guilty of the offence charged. The evidence shows that the respondent in this case had been absenting herself regularly from her home in the evenings, not returning until a very late hour, and that she informed her husband that she had grown tired of him, preferred some one else, and proposed, I think, to live with some one else. Immediately after that statement, she separated from her husband, and the evidence shows that for a period of a year she lived in a house, I think in Ossington avenue, in the city of Toronto, the only other occupant of which was a man by the name of Hillyard, whom she introduced to her neighbours as her brother, while the evidence shows that he was not, in fact, her brother. It seems to me that that is a combination of circumstances which raises only one inference, and, so far as I am concerned I have no hesitation in saying that of all the cases that have been considered by the Private Bills Committee this session, I entertain less doubt with respect to the petitioner's right to divorce in this case than in any other.
Preamble carried on division, and Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

House in Committee on Bill No. 234, for the relief of Lenore Power.-Mr. MacNutt. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)
On section 1:

This case was brought
to my attention by a number of gentlemen some days ago, and I took the trouble to read the evidence which had been submitted to the Senate Committee in connection with it. I must say that, in my humble judgment, there is absolutely no evidence in this case to justify the granting of divorce. I think that considerable care should be taken in passing these Bills. I consider that when there is no direct evidence of the one fact which is necessary to give this Parliament jurisdiction to grant divorce, there should be a superabundance of indirect evidence, on which we could come to a conclusion that the party was guilty of the offence. I am-not going into the evidence in this case. As a matter of fact, the person who is named as co-respondent came before the Senate Committee, and absolutely denied that anything had taken place between herself and Power which would justify the granting of divorce. She underwent a most severe cross-examin
a/tion, and her evidence was not weakened in the least. I do not see where there is anything on which we can ground the assumption or conclusion that the one vital fact, which is necessary in a case of this kind, has been proven, or even attempted to be proven. I do not think that the Parliament of Canada should undertake to deal lightly with matters of this kind, especially on very flimsy evidence. As a lawyer, I consider that tnere is absolutely no evidence to justify this Parliament in passing this Bill. For these reasons I am opposing the bul, and I would advise hon. gentlemen if they have not read the evidence, to read it before casting their votes on this Bill.

Having taken a considerable part in the discussion of this Bill in the Private Bills Committee, I feel impelled to say a few words in connection with it. At the outset, I wish to say that I entirely agree with what my hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) has said. I do not think that the petitioner, either upon her own evidence or upon the whole evidence, is entitled to a divorce. I do not propose, for various reasons, among others, that the evidence is somewhat revolting, to go into detail; but perhaps I may be allowed to refer to what appeared to me to be two or three striking illustrations of the weakness of the case in the petitioner's story. Her only evidence is that a confession was made by her husband, apparently in a moment of sorrow or repentance.
To herself?

To herself. She gave evidence to a confession made by her husband, and that is absolutely the only evidence adduced by her in support of her application. On page 11, she says:
He admitted that he had got too familiar with May.
In cross-examination on page 14, she puts it in this way:
He said: ' It was my fault, I tried to get too familiar with May.'
I cannot conceive it possible that any person believing that adultery had been committed would have made the statement which she made in cross-examination, that he had said he had tried to get too familiar, for I judge that in that case he had a little more than tried. When we look at other parts of the evidence, we find that, in answer to the Chairman, she said:
Q. You understood perfectly well from what he said that he had connection with her at that time?
Her answer was:
I certainly drew that inference.

Nowhere is there stronger evidence than that she drew an inference. As against that evidence you have the positive contradiction by the young woman herself. There is another most striking feature to be found in the evidence. The offence was committed, if committed at all, on the 13th of November, which was a Wednesday. She learned of it on the following Sunday. On the 25th of November, some days later, she gives this young girl, whom she blames, this certificate of character:
Miss Dyer has been with me for nearly three years as companion. I have found her industrious, capable and trustworthy, and will be glad to answer any inquiries. Address, Mrs. Power, Cobourg. Am parting with her because I cannot keep a companion any longer.
(Sgd.) Lenore Dennis Power.
I can only come to one conclusion that, when the petitioner gave that certificate of character, she could not have had divorce in her mind at all, and that divorce must have been an afterthought. I might have hesitated to take up the time of the House, were it not for the closeness of the vote in the committee. This case was discussed twice in the committee. It reached us in error before the Bill had been read a second time and referred, and the vote w-r-s seven to three against granting the divorce. It reached us again, having that very evening had its second reading. On that occasion the vote was 6 to 6 and a gentleman of the committee, who at first did not vote, in the epd decided to vote and gave the casting in favour of the Bill.
I regret the practice that prevails in Canada as to granting divorces; but, as long as these Bills must come before a Private Bills Committee, and as long as members of that committee have to take the responsibility of acting uphn the committee, it appears to me that we must try to do our duty. I do not think there is any evidence to warrant us in granting this Bill and I would think it is as easy to put a Bill through this Parliament as to get divorces in Reno, if this Bill goes through.

With great deference
to the views expressed by my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Boys), I believe that the evidence adduced before the Senate Committee in this case and considered by the Private Bills Committee, proves that the respondent was guilty of the offence charged. Had I considered only the evidence which the petitioner gave in regard to the admission which her husband made to her of his conduct, I would not have been disposed to vote for the divorce; but the co-respondent was put upon the stand and was examined by counsel representing the respondent. The co-respondent corroborated every detail of ' Mr. BOYS.
the admission which the respondent made to the petitioner, except with regard to the actual fact of adultery. There is no doubt at all but that, if the admission which the respondent made to the petitioner is true, the offence was committed, and would be held to have been committed by any court of law in this country. I shall read just the material evidence on page 11, a3 follows:
He said: 'Well, last Wednesday evening I made a fool of myself. I was sitting downstairs, and May was sitting there, and I pulled her over on my lap-she did not seem to object very much; she sat there for some time; she did not seem to have very much on in the way of clothing, and I got very inquisitive and investigated.' He said, ' I put my hands up her clothes, and found that she had no draw ers on.' He said, ' she sat there for some time, and then she said she wanted to go to bed; so I carried her upstairs to her bedroom with my arms around her bare body.' I said, ' and you went to bed with her ? ' He said, ' No, not then, I didn't.' He said, ' I went downstairs and I drank some whisky, and when I went upstairs again I undressed and I went to her bed.'
If that evidence were given in any court of law, it certainly would be taken as-evidence of the commission of adultery. One can well understand that the young girl would perhaps not admit the commission of the actual fact, but that is the only difference between the statement of the co-respondent and of the petitioner in this case. It is for that reason that I voted for the granting of this divorce.

There is no evidence
here to be corroborated. The confession which this husband made to his wife is simply a confession of familiarity with a third party; this young girl admits all that familiarity, but swears most positively, even under an hour's cross-examination, that nothing outside of a little familiarity took place between them. I intend to call for a vote on this question before it passes this committee.

It has
been said that in this case there is sufficient evidence to convince a court of justice. I disagree with that entirely. I have read over this case carefully, and have given it serious consideration. I am satisfied there is no evidence which would convince any judge that adultery was committed. There is no question whatever that there was an attempt, and the man would morally be just as blameworthy as if he had succeeded; but, if we have to decide here that there is actual adultery, there is no evidence whatever on that point. Our duty is to dispose of this Bill on such evidence as has been submitted, and in view of that I am prepared to vote against this divorce being granted. The man him-

self does not admit positively, and the petitioner merely says that from what he said she inferred that certain things had happened.

I am not a member of the Private Bills Committee, but I heard a good deal of the discussion and afterwards glanced over the evidence. In the first place, none of these gentlemen have referred to the fact that the man admitted, and it is not denied by the girl, that he was in a positive state of drunkenness at the time the alleged act occurred. The whole secret lies in this fact that, according to the evidence, this woman is simply tired of the man. She has an income of $1,400 a year; she is a prospective heiress to some $60,000. In my opinion, had the man not been worth a dollar, the girl would have been turned out of the house and the man turned to work, too. Suppose this man had been prosecuted, if it were a criminal offence, what is the evidence? The positive denial of the man that anything improper happened-by improper I mean adultery- and also the positive denial of the girl. If a divorce is granted, this girl is branded for all time to come. The couple are not very old. So far as I am concerned, I shall vote against granting a divorce, and probably in a year they will both come to their senses.

As I have been saying
in this Parliament for the last ten years all this goes to show that this is not the tribunal in which such a case should be tried. I have no fault to find with any hon. member who says that there is no case against the man, and I am just as honest in my view that there has been a strong case made out. I base my opinion on the evidence and the correspondence, and I base it more on what the petitioner did not swear to than what she did swear to.
Oh.

The whole case illustrates the unfairness of this House of Commons sitting as a court of appeal on evidence they did not hear and without knowing how the witnesses deported themselves on the stand, which in most cases is a matter of the greatest importance. The Senate Committee gave this matter their earnest consideration, and they came to the conclusion that a divorce should be granted.

Does the hon. gentleman
think that a jury should decide on the evidence that was not given rather than on the evidence that was given?

The hon. member is not serious in asking such a question. My hon. friend from York, N.B. (Mr. Crocket), who is a good lawyer, one of the best lawyers in the House, and who is chairman of the committee, gave you his opinion as to the legal result of the evidence, and I entirelv concur with him. In my judgment, the woman co-respondent in the case simply perjured herself like a lady.
Was there a confession of adultery?

I do not intend in this public place to discuss the details of the case.	[DOT]
Mr, BENNETT (Calgary): The late Lord Hannen, who was chairman of the Divorce Court in England for many years, said that m such cases as this if on the evidence before the court the circumstances were equally compatible with innocence or guilt, the jury should find the accused innocent. On the evidence in this case, the facts are equally consistent with innocence or guilt, and I propose to give the accused the benefit of the doubt. The case against this man is that he himself first brought his wife's attention to a state of facts which he said constituted wrongdoing on his part. He telephoned her, and she came from Toronto, and he met her at the station, and she' says he there confessed to improper relations with 'this girl; but stated that the improper relations were only familiarity and were not criminal. You have the positive denial of the girl charged as co-respondent, and you have the evidence that the husband told the wife herself in the first instance that there was familiarity, but not crim-nality. These facts are as compatible with innocence as with guilt, and I would have to go further than any case I have read in the books were I to find the man guilty of the offence charged against him.

House again in Committee on the proposed resolutions respecting the granting of the subsidies therein mentioned to the Canadian Northern Railway Company. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)

When the committee
rose I had about concluded, but as an hon. member has asked me for an explanation of the clause placed in the various subsidy Acts, I think it is but fair I should make clear what I had in mind. The clause which, except in this case, has invariably

been placed in subsidy Acts, is in the present resolution and reads as follows:
That the granting of such subsidies and the receipt thereof by the respective companies shall be subject to the condition that the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada may at all times provide and secure to other companies such running powers, traffic arrangements and other rights as will afford to all railways connecting with the railway and bridges so subsidized reasonable and proper facilities in exercising such running power, fair and reasonable traffic arrangements with connecting companies, and equal mileage rates between all such connecting railways; and the said board shall have absolute control, at all times, over the rates and tolls to be levied and taken by any of the companies, or upon any of the railways and bridges hereby subsidized:	Provided always
that any decision of the said board made under this section may be at any time varied, changed or rescinded by the Governor in Council, as he deems just and proper.
An amendment was moved by myself last year when the Canadian Northern Pacific railway subsidy was going through, that this clause be inserted in the Act. That was defeated in the House. What I propose to mQve at some stage of the present resolution or of the Bill to be based upon it is that this clause be added, except that the name of the Canadian Northern Pacific railway be inserted, making it apply to that particular part of this transcontinental line as it will apply to other parts. I know the Prime Minister will say that this is a different company and we are not now subsidizing that company. But I submit that it is the same system, owned by the same parties, and will form part of the transcontinental line. And this is probably the last opporunity we shall have of imposing on this transcontinental system an obligation that this, like other transcontinental systems, shall be under the Board of Railway Commissioners. I merely make this explanation so that the Prime Minister may know that I propose to move this amendment at some time in the proceedings.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. L. BORDEN (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is debating the same matter we had under consideration last year-the effect of the agreement of this company with the Government of British Columbia that it will not prosecute any appeal to the Board of Railway Commissioners?
Yes, and that the rates shall" not be under the Board of Railway Commissioners as the British Columbia Government have provided some other tribunal to fix the rates on this road.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As I recollect the matter last year, the provisions of the Railway Act seemed to indicate that there would be Mr. GRAHAM.
jurisdiction in respect of through traffic. The answer made was that the company had agreed that it would not invoke that jurisdiction. That was the situation as I recollect it.

The company agreed that it would not invoke that jurisdiction, and my contention is that the decision of the Privy Council renders that part_ of the Railway Act ultra vires which is relied upon to give jurisdiction to the Railway Commissioners over rates on a line which is partly a provincial line.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: So far as that is concerned, I think the hon. gentleman will agree with me that this system must be regarded as a whole, and that in the end it must be brought under the ownership and control of one company.

What about British
Columbia ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I will come to that in a moment. If this road is to fulfil the purpose of a transcontinental railway, it is abundantly evident that the whole system must in the future, and the not distant future, be brought under the ownership and control of one company; and it must come to this Parliament for that purpose. When it does come to this Parliament for that purpose, Parliament will have ample jurisdiction to insist that the whole line, from the Pacific to Quebec, or wherever the eastern terminus may be, shall be under the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada. I have no apprehension whatever as to what the practical result will be in that regard. Further, looking over the debate of last year, I find that I argued then -and I see no reason to depart from my conclusion now, unless there has been in the meantime some decision such as that on which my hon. friend relies-that under the provisions of the Railway Act, the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada has jurisdiction over through traffic on this line. I admit what my hon. friend contends for, that it is desirable that the whole of this line, not only with respect to through traffic, but with respect to all traffic, should be under the jurisdiction of one tribunal. But the circumstances attending the granting of aid by the province of British Columbia were inconsistent with that result, so far as this line was within the limits of the province of British Columbia and was aided by the province; and we did not attempt to over-ride or interfere with that last year, for the reason that, so far as through traffice was concerned, we thought there was perfect jurisdiction and control in the Board of Railway Commissioners. But, whether that be the case or not. the road must eventually come under the ownership and control, and

under the operation, of one company, if it is to be a real transcontinental line.
My hon. friend has agreed in our appreciation of the status of this road. As far back as 1903, when we were discussing the proposal of the late Administration to build a new transcontinental railway, I said from my place in this House, that the Canadian Northern railway system had, even at that time, attained the status of a transcontinental mad. Having regard to its subsequent development and progress, there is no doubt that the Canadian Northern railway must be regarded as one of the three great transcontinental railways of Canada.
I concur entirely in the appreciation of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) of the importance of the transportation system of this country to the development and progress of Canada. It is of course quite apparent that the development and progress of this country in recent years have been due to a number of great causes, one of which has been the abundance and variety of our natural resources and the capacity and energy of our people in developing them. But there are two other great causes which must not be lost sight of, and without which the progress of Canada during the past fifteen or twenty years would have been much less than it has been. These two causes are the development of transportation-the enormous pace at which railway construction has proceeded in this country-and the very great volume of our immigration. Railway construction and immigration have had a great deal to do, as every hon. gentleman in this House knows, with the progress and development of this country during many years in the past. I concur'with what my hon. friend the member for South Renfrew said as to the strenuous efforts the Can-ad ian people have made, and the tremendous sacrifices they have been willing to undergo for the purpose of extending and developing the transportation systems of this country. Economical and rapid transportation facilities are more necessary to Canada than perhaps to any other country in the world. We have all of these vast natural resources scattered over a country as large as Europe; we have a sparse population, divided to a certain extent into isolated communities, and scattered over the face of our great country. The problem of transportation begins at the farm, the factory, or any other centre of production, and does not cease until it reaches the market, whether it be in this or in some other country.
Another thing we ought to recognize is that the difficulties incurred in creating in this country a transportation system are much greater than they are in the
country to the south of us. We have some 800 miles of territory north of Lake Superior; territory upon and around which there is no local traffic, and which wild probably not contain any very great population for many years to come. Therefore, in considering the project of building a transcontinental railway in Canada, you have to take into account 800 or 900 miles of road that must be built and operated, but which, so far as local traffic is concerned, can afford to the company no remuneration whatever, and which is to a certain extent a handicap upon the operating facilities of the road. Under all these circumstances, it seems to me that the progress and development of this country in transportar tion has been much greater than any of us could reasonably have anticipated twenty-five or thfrty years ago. It is a wonderful thing that the Canadian people have been able to accomplish all that has been accomplished. I know that in many parts of the country, particularly in western Canada, there has been a great deal of complaint as to the operation of some of our railways, but that has been largely due to the fact that an enormous crop has to be carried in a very few weeks. The problem before the railway companies of Canada is very much like the problem placed before a tram line company in a large city, where 10,000 people within a very small area wish to get on the ears within a very short space of time.
There is one other thing that ought to be taken into account in considering the proposals of the Government now submitted to Parliament, and that is, not only that the cost of labour and material has greatly increased within the past eight or ten years, but that unexpected difficulties in respect of railway construction and operation have arisen. The construction of this road through the Rocky mountains and along the northern shore of -lake Superior has proved unexpectedly difficult and expensive, and in addition to that we have had during the past twelve or eighteen months a condition of financial stringency which I believe has not been equalled and certainly has not been exceeded during the past twenty years. It is a stringency which is not confined to this country, but is world-wide, and therefore affects the very source from which Canada has drawn capital for her railway development during many years in the past.
I have spoken of these difficulties, but they are not sufficient to stay, and must not be permitted to stay, our progress in railway development in this country. There is a very large immigration flowing into Canada; I believe it ran to about 400,000 people last year. We have enormous areas in all parts of the country, particularly in the West, which have not yet been

brought under cultivation. I am speaking only from recollection, but I think with some accuracy, when I say that out of about 500,000,000 acres of land in the prairie provinces of Canada it is estimated that some 250,000,000 are arable, and of the 250,000,000 which are arable I believe that not more than fifteen or twenty millions have up to the present time been brought under the plough. Therefore we have this enormous extent of arable land capable of producing sufficient grain not only for this country, but almost for the world, and that land awaits the coming of the husbandman. Persons from a great many different parts of the world, particularly from Great Britain and the United States, are going into that country for the purpose of undertakig the labours that are necessary in order that this land may be made productive. Under these circumstances I entirely concur with what my hon. friend the member for South Renfrew said so well, that under no circumstances should the Parliament of Canada, as representing the people of this country, permit this great railway enterprise to collapse or even to have its progress unduly checked or stayed. It was with that consideration that these proposals have been submitted to Parliament.	.
I think the hon. Minister of Finance was perhaps slightly misunderstood when he directed the -attention of the committee to certain statistics as to the provision of the necessary capital for the construction of the Canadian Northern railway. I must at once admit that when the statistics which have been laid before this committee by the Minister of Finance were brought to my attention, I was very much surprised. It has been popularly supposed, and I myself was under the impression, that very much the largest proportion of all the money that had been raised for the purpose of constructing the Canadian Northern railway system hM been raised by means of bonds and securities guaranteed by the Government'of Canada or by the governments of several of the provinces. But when the actual facts were laid before me I found that these securities-and I am not speaking for the moment of the subsidies-amounted altogether to no less than $265,000,000, and I found that of that amount $145,000,000 had not been guaranteed either by the Government of Canada or by the Government of any province, and the balance, $120,000,000, had been guaranteed either by the Government of Canada or by the Government of some province. Of the $120,000,000 of securities which had been guaranteed by one Government or the other, only $58,000,000 had been guaranteed by the Government of Canada. The only result of that, therefore, was that out of $265,000,000 of securities which had been Mr. BORDEN.
issued for the purpose of constructing this great transcontinental system, no more than $58,000,000, or a little more than one-fifth, had been guaranteed by the people of Canada as a whole. I want that particular circumstance to be understood by the committee because, so far as I am concerned, it reveals to me a condition which I did not anticipate, and of which I was ignorant up to that time. I had supposed that a very much -larger proportion had been guaranteed either by one Government or the other.
As the Minister of Railways and Canals has observed, we have had a great many subsidy Bills before parliament within the last fifteen or twenty years, and whichever Government was in power, a certain policy has been followed of giving subsidies up to the amount of $6,400 a mile, assuming the construction of the road to have cost a certain amount.	That has been given
almost as a matter of course, provided the road supposed to be constructed appealed to the Government as one which would serve the public necessity in any reasonable way. I have here a list of roads to which such subsidies have been granted during the last eight or ten years. The list is very long, and the roads are of a varied character indeed, running from little branches of three, four or half a dozen miles, to lines of 500 or 1,000 miles forming important parts of our great transportation systems. There has not, so far as I am aware, been any unwillingness on the part of any Government or of any parliament to give aid up to that amount to any road which seemed reasonably calculated to serve the public interest in the way of transportation. That I venture to assert, without fear of contradiction, fairly indicates the policy which has been carried out by the Government of the right hon. gentleman opposite as well as by the Conservative Government which preceded him before 1896. Then, coming to the particular proposals now submitted for the consideration of the committee, we have not in this instance a road of the unimportant-character of many of those that have been subsidized during the past quarter of a century; we have a road which constitutes the main line of a great transcontinental railway system the completion of which, as the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has said, and said truly, has become of vital importance to the country and to the completion of which we are committed, provided that the demands upon us are not of an unreasonable nature. One would think that under these circumstances the granting of a subsidy of $6,400 per mile, such as has been allowed to any one of the varied

roads that have been subsidized by Parliament during the past twenty-five or thirty years, would not be objected to under the conditions and in view o! the circumstances to which I have alluded. It is certainly a fact that the portion of the road, for which the subsidy is now asked, is of an exceptionally expensive character, perhaps not so expensive as the road to which Parliament granted a subsidy of $12,000 only last session but still twice or even three times as expensive as some of the roads to which subsidies have been granted during the period I have mentioned. The amount of $6,400 per mile has been granted to many of these roads, the cost of which has not exceeded $20,000 or $25,000 per mile.
Surely, so far as the subsidy to this road is concerned, in view of the greatly increased cost of its construction, no hon. gentleman in this House would say that Parliament, in view of the importance of the road and in view of the conditions to which I have alluded, ought to refuse this reasonable measure of aid. The aid which we propose does not stop there, because we have asked Parliament to assent, not only to the ordinary subsidy of $6,400 per mile but to an additional amount of $5,600 per mile, making $12,000 per mile in all. If we base our proposals simply upon the importance of the road as contrasted with many roads to which $6,400 per mile has been granted and upon the consideration that this aid is in respect of its main line and not in respect of branch lines which form its feeders, our proposals would be justified. But we bring also to the attention of Parliament, not only the greatly increased cost of railway construction during these later years, but also the condition of financial stringency which has made it almost impossible for those interested in railway construction in this country to provide the means for continuing their work. Stoppage of construction would entail exceed-irghT unfortunate results not only to the company-because its interests are not to be considered except so far as'the public interest is involved in them-but to the whole country. We propose, as we did last year in respect of another portion of the same line, that a subsidy, not of $6,400 per mile but of $12,000 per mile, should bp granted to this railway system and we believe that this aid is necessary to secure the completion of this road. Parliament must take account of the situation which confronts the country and confronts the railway company under present conditions. I have made pretty careful investigation as to the efforts of this company and of she Grand Trunk Pacific Company to accomplish the financing necessary to enable them to keep on with their work in the future as thev have been carrying it on in the past.
I need not enter into detail, as regards the efforts which have been made to provide the capital necessary for the completion of these two roads. I think that hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House will appreciate the undesirability of going too much into details of that ch&raoter. It is enough to say that with respect not only to railway enterprises, but to enterprises which, under ordinary conditions, would be regarded as absolutely first-class securities in the money markets of the world, it has been almost absolutely impossible to raise money.
But we did not stop there, so far as this railway is concerned, although the considerations which I have brought to	the attention of the committee
would seem to me suflicient to appeal to the judgment of any man who did not desire that the progress and development of this country, especially in railway construction, should be brought to any sudden or undesirable check at this moment. The sum of $5,600 per mile, being the difference between the ordinary subsidy of $6,400 per mile and the subsidy now asked for, $12,000 per mile, is more than covered by the sum of $7,000,000 of capital stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, which is to be transferred to the Minister of Finance as fully paid-up stock, and which is to give this country a certain interest at least in the future prosperity of that road, if its future should be crowned with success. If this country continues to develop in the future as it has done in the past-and I think none of us have reason to doubt that

it seems to me exceedingly probable that that asset will be of great value to this country. We did not accept stock in any of those minor companies, the value of which, even in the future, might be more or less uncertain. We asked for $7,000,000 of the capital stock of the parent company itself, the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and whether or not that has anything more than an indeterminate value at the present time, I do think that there is not only the possibility, but the probability, that at some time in the future, and perhaps in the not distant future, it may be of very real and tangible value.
My hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) made some inquiry as to whether or not the Government of this country is to be represented on the Board of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. I have no doubt whatever that that result would be brought about without any difficulty, if it were worth while. During the period that we have been in office, and for some time before, the Government of Canada has been represented on the Board of the



Grand Trunk Pacific by one gentleman at least; I am not sure whether by more than one.
By one.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am bound to say that up to the present time I have not seen any marked or material advantage resulting to this country from the presence on that board of the gentleman, whoever he may be. He is there, and he represents the country; but I do not know that there is any very distinct or peculiar advantage arising from his presence.
The question has been fairly put by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House: Why did you not do this by means of a loan, as in the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and why do you propose to give this large subsidy to this company, whereas, in respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific, you are merely proposing a loan ? Well, my hon. friend the Minister Minister of Finance went pretty fully into that,	and	I do not desire
to repeat at any length what he said. But perhaps there are one or two things which he did not emphasize in the way I would like to emphasize them. In the first instance, there is something to be said for the position that as those roads are to be competitive roads in the West, some reasonable basis of equality of treatment should be accorded to them, if you recognize them as transcontinental railways to the completion of which the interests of this country are in some measure committed. There is something perhaps to be said for that position, although I do not urge it as the main position. Whatever that argument may be worth, and no small weight is to be attached to it, it must be apparent to every hon. gentleman who has heard this discussion that in respect of the line from Montreal to the Pacific coast, this system, for which these subsidies are proposed to be granted, will have received a great deal less direct financial aid in the way of cash subsidies than the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company received in respect of the line from Winnipeg to the coast. The figures which have been given make that abundantly apparent, so far as the main line is concerned. [DOT]
I know my hon. friend the member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) did bring into consideration certain lands which had been bought by the Canadian Northern Railway Company, or by one-of its subsidiary companies, for the roads which had been chartered in the West, and which had received those land grants. These were not direct grants to the Canadian Northern Railway Company, or to any of its subsidiary companies. It was open to any man in this House, or to any railway company in Canada, to purchase those enterprises and Mr. BORDEN.
I .	

to acquire those land grants in the same way that the Canadian Northern Railway Company acquired them. So far as I understand, and so far as my information goes, they were bought in the open market, so to speak. Those enterprises could be purchased and one of these companies did purchase them, and it has acquired whatever advantage was to be derived from them. But they were not direct grants to the Canadian Northern Railway Company, or to any of its subsidiary companies, in the first instance.
Then, you have the consideration to which I have alluded, that even if you grant this subsidy, this road will not be in as good a position, so far as direct financial aid is concerned, as the road which has been subsidized and assisted from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast. There is another consideration in connection with that, which perhaps the Minister of Finance did not emphasize. The aid was granted to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company under such conditions that not one dollar can be deducted from the amount payable by Canada to that company for the carriage of mails; but so far as the Canadian Northern Railway Company is concerned, every dollar of the subsidy is subject to that condition. That is another very distinct position of advantage which is held not only by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company but by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company as well, in contradistinction to the condition which has been imposed on the Canadian Northern Railway Company; and the payment of three per cent upon the amount of those subsidies comes to no inconsiderable sum, even upon the standard of $6,400 per mile.
The Minister of Finance has shown-and I have the figures under my hand to establish the same point if it were necessary
that, so far as assistance by guarantees of securities is concerned, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company from Winnipeg to the coast has received from this Dominion more assistance than the Canadian Northern system from Montreal to the coast._ Having regard to these considerations, it does not seem to me that the present proposal is unreasonable.
Hon. gentlemen opposite say: why do you not accomplish this result by way of loan rather than by subsidy? The answer I have given to that seems to be sufficient; but, apart from that, the question of making a loan to the Canadian Northern railway system must take account of all the necessities of that road in respect to provision for its future expenditure. The Canadian Northern will have to expend, as I am informed on the best authority, about $40,000,000 in providing for its terminals ; and hon. gentlemen opposite must bear in mind that, with the growth

and development of our cities and the exceeding great advance in the cost of land in these cities, the cost of terminals whether in eastern or in western Canada, has advanced enormously during recent years. If we were toi say to the Canadian Northern Railway Company:	The aid we
give you must be by way of loan and we cannot place you on an equality, so far as direct cash aid is concerned, with even the Grand Trunk Pacific, although your line to Montreal is about 1,000 miles longer than the Grand Trunk Pacific line from Winnipeg to the coast; if we were to take that position, we would have to assume a certain responsibility for all the future financing of that company. If we were to make a loan to that company and to take securities which would be worthy of the name, we would so involve the question of the future financing of that company that the country must in the end assume responsibility for the raising of the money necessary to complete its line. When you take the one alternative and the other particularly as the Canadian Northern Railway Company professes itself able, under ordinary conditions, to raise all the money that may be necessary for the completion of its line, and when you take into consideration the fact that the aid we are now giving to that road is less, so far as direct financial assistance is concerned, than that which has been given to a competitive road with 1,000 miles less of line, it would have been unreasonable and unwise for us to say that we would not grant the aid to the Canadian Northern railway up to the standard of assistance which has been accorded to another transcontinental railway, and that we would insist upon asking this Parliament to undertake a responsibility which would involve our taking care of all of the future finances of the Canadian Northern Railway Company.
I for one was reluctant to ask Parliament to assume that responsibility. I thought it would be a more reasonable course to say to Parliament: This is a competing line with the Grand Trunk Pacific and in respect to its main line, 1,000 miles longer than that of the Grand Trunk Pacific from Winnipeg to the coast, we are proposing to Parliament that Canada shall assist this system to the same extent as it has already assisted the Grand Trunk Pacific from Winnipeg to the coast. I venture to think that that view ought to commend itself to hon. gentlemen opposite. However that may be it was a question of alternatives, and I can assure hon. gentlemen on both sides that we made a very careful study of the whole situation before we decided upon giving the aid contained in these proposals; and we came to the conclusion after the most careful study and investigation we could give to what undoubtedly was a question of some complexity, that, in view of all the conditions, the aid for which

Parliament should be asked at the present juncture should be by way of equalizing the direct financial assistance, and not by way of undertaking a responsibility which would make it incumbent upon us to look after the finances of the Canadian Northern in the future Had we adopted the latter course we would have tied up their whole system with a security such as Parliament might reasonably require for a large loan and the result would have been that which I have indicated. If ever a proposition has been damned with faint praise, the proposition of the Government which is now before this committee has been damned by the speech of the right hon. the Prime Minister; because, a speech more inconsistent with the proposition before Parliament, I never heard delivered by a Prime Minister of Canada. I am very much inclined to think that the right hon. gentleman is in accord with many of his followers-if rumour in the corridors is correct, really a majority-who are opposed to this scheme entirely.
Speak for yourself.

Speaking for myself, I
am opposed to it; and, speaking for hon. gentlemen opposite, I am very much inclined to think, having listened to the speech of their leader, that there is at least no enthusiasm in favor of it on the other side. It was left to the Minister of Finance to make an enthusiastic speech in favour of this proposition, and I am not very much surprised that he did so in view of the circumstances surrounding his appointment as Minister of Finance, because we all know in the province of Ontario how that happened.
Tell us.

The Canadian Northern
Railway Company is supposed to be controlled by Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann, knights of the realm.

Who made
them knights?

The gentleman who controls the Canadian Northern Railway Company is like Sir Joseph Porter, First Lord of the Admiralty in the comic opera ' Pinafore ': he sits at his desk and never goes to sea. Mr. Zebulon A. Lash is the gentleman who controls the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and he is the gentleman who got up the round robin and in-

duced Mr. White to sign it, with Sir Byron Walker and the other noble eighteen Liberals in the province of Ontario, against the reciprocity resolution.
Where were you?

I was against the reciprocity proposition, but I was not going around with brass bands. I did what I thought was right in the interests of the country, and I have never had occasion to regret it. Mr. Zebulon A. Lash was the gentleman who got up the round robin, and who got the Minister of Finance to sign it. He was the man who made him Minister of Finance. Now he is coming for his reward. He is the gentleman who controls the Canadian Northern Railway Company, if that is any information to hon. gentlemen opposite.
Many years ago in the province of Ontario, before the Judicature Act was enforced, we had a system of pleading which was called special pleading. I had occasion to be a law student in the office of Hon. Lewis Wallbridge, who was one of the most expert pleaders we had in the province.

You have
been an apt pupil.

It was very technical
and very interesting; but I think I could give my hon. friend the Minister of Finance a fairly good record as being a special pleader, because as a special pleader he excelled himself this afternoon in the way in which he manipulated the figures in connection with this whole transaction, in the first place he endeavoured to show that the-late Government had granted great concessions to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company by guaranteeing their bonds, and he wound up by saying that a guarantee of bonds was no responsibility whatever to the country. I do not think we need bother about that any further. Let us come down to what is the crux of the situation. After many questions, after many interrogatories, after many interruptions, we succeeded in forcing the hon. Minister of Finance to tell us the amount of the subsidies which the Canadian Northern Railway Company got. Finally we succeeded in compelling him to state what had become of the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. What has become of it? He says $25,000,000 is held by the company in trust, until 1916 if I understand him correctly.

I think that is the
statement he made.

Then until 1916 the
holders of the debenture stock can exchange it if they like for the common stock of the company. Is there a man living who Mr. GERMAN.
would imagine that any person, holding debenture stock which is secured by mortgage on the whole assets of the company, will change that stock between now and 1916 for the common stock of the company? The result will be that in 1916 that $25,000,000 of stock will be released and will belong - to Mackenzie & Mann, just as the $45,000,000 belongs at this moment to these gentlemen. The hon. Minister of Finance made the statement this afternoon that $45,000,000 of that stock-I am under that impression, but I am in the judgment of what ' Hansard ' says to-morrow- has been handed out to Mackenzie & Mann as the construction company of the Canadian Northern Railway Company.
He did not say that.

I am in the judgment of what ' Hansard ' says to-morrow; but, whether he said it or not, that is exactly what has been done. They have got $45,000,000 of the stock, and besides that they have made in the construction of that railroad at least $10,000,000. They have been the contractors, the construction company; they have built the whole road from one end to the other at their own prices without any competition; subletting the contracts to whomsoever they saw fit. In addition to that they will control the other $25,000,000, when it is released from trust at the end of 1916. Then this company, controlled by these gentlemen, comes to this Parliament and says: We want you to give us $15,000,000 more. I have no quarrel with the Canadian Northern Railway Company or any other railway company. I am willing to do everything I can to aid this company and every other company to carry on their transactions profitably, in order to build up this country; but I protest against two men in this country simply exploiting a railway proposition as these two men have exploited the Canadian Northern railway. I say that advisedly, because I know what I am talking about. They own the company; they have made many millions of dollars in the construction of the road, and the public is paying the price. I do not think we should go any further in regard to the matter.
The Canadian Pacific railway has been discussed. What happened in regard to it? Donald Smith, George Stephen, R. B. Angus and Duncan McIntyre were the promoters. They were wealthy men. When they came to the Parliament of Canada to borrow $25,000,000 they had put every dollar they possessed in that road. If it had been a failure, they would have been bankrupt. They did not come to the people of Canada and say: Build a road for us. They had the faith of their convictions. Why do
11/1)1

these gentlemen not do the same? If they want money from the people of Canada to build this railroad, let them put their own money in it for a while. Do they expect the people of Canada to build a transcontinental railway for them, and to give it to them after it is built? My hon. friend the Minister of Finance said this afternoon that we were giving great subventions to the Grand Trunk Pacific. As the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) said: ' When that road is built we shall own a large part of it.' We are putting our money in a transaction which the people of Canada will own. What do we own in connection with the Canadian Northern Railway Company? It is said, we shall have $7,000,000 of their stock. For my part, I do not believe that .the Government of Canada should take stock in any railway company. The Government might as well take stock in a manufacturing company. If this company wants money from the people of Canada, I believe they can get it if they offer what they would give to any person else. If they come here with such a proposition, I certainly shall be willing to help them in any way I can. I do not however, believe,. as a matter of fact, that $15,000,000 is worth a sheet of paper to them now. I think that $30,000,000 or $35,000,000 might be of some advantage to them, and if they come and ask $35,000,000 of the people of Canada and give security, I believe that the people would be willing to let them have it for the purpose of maintaining a great transcontinental road such as this. But I for one will not be a party to handing over to this company $15,000,000 under the present circumstances. The stock of this company is controlled by two or three men who have madie millions out of the construction.
But I desire to come to another question, which, I think, is of equal if not of greater importance than even this question of the subsidy to this transcontinental line. This company is building, and has nearly completed, a line of railway between the city of Toronto and the city of Ottawa, and this Parliament is asked to give a subsidy of $6,400 a mile towards that road. On what grounds such a proposition is made, I really cannot understand. There is no use in hon. members sayiaig tha/t we have subsidized other roads. The line of the Canadian Pacific railway between here and Toronto was the original line. I believe it was at one time called the Ontario and Quebec, and was built under subsidy. Why was the subsidy given? Because the road Tan through what was then a wilderness, a new country. The Canadian Pacific railway _ eventually took over the road and took it over with the advantage of the subsidy. The principle upon which subsidies have always been granted is to afford aid to a railway company for the construction of a railway opening a new part of the country. We want these unopened parts of the country served with railways in order that settlers ni/ay go in and develop the resources of those sections. Men _ will not invest their money in building a railway into an unopened and unsettled country without aid1, and consequently the Dominion and provincial governments give aid to these, people. But why a subsidy should be granted to a railway company for constructing a line through the heart of the province of Ontario, reaching every town and city in the eastern part of the province which is prosperous and growing, I do not understand. That road will pay from1, the minute it is opened. From the time the first train runs on the Canadian Northern Ontario railway between Ottawa and Toronto, that road will be a paying proposition and will help to pay off the liabilities of the parent company. Then, why in the name of all that is sensible should this Government be asked to give them a subsidy? Suppose that before beginning to build a road they had come and asked a subsidy to build such a road, would any man in this House have supported the proposition? They would have said:	Go
ahead and build your road; there is plenty of scope and your enterprise will pay from the beginning. At one end of the road is the city of Toronto with a population of between 500,000 and 600,000 and at the other is the city of Ottawa with a population of 100,000. The line goes through Cobourg, Port Hope, Belleville and Kingston, all the largest places in this part of the province of Ontario. And it will go through the wealthy country of the province. To subsidize such a railway, I submit, is too absurd for consideration. I, for one, will not agree to it. The Minister of Railways agreed with me this afternoon that if the London and Tillsonburg Railway Company did not earn their subsidy before the time came for renewal, the subsidy should he refused them. Why? Because they are building through a well-settled country.
No, because I do not believe in voting subsidies and letting them stay on the paper unearned. I believe in building.

If a road is entitled to a subsidy for building, it is entitled to that subsidy whenever it builds, and so I cannot quite see the distinction the hon. gentleman makes. But .the point I contend for is that the line of railway designated in this resolution offers no justification for the subsidy. And, so strongly do I feel on this subject, that I move that clause 1 of this resolution be struck out.

I am sure the members of the committee must have been struck with the rather modest way in which this matter has been dealt with by hon. gentlemen composing the Government. One could not help being impressed with the changed conditions that are so apparent in these hon. gentlemen when they approach the consideration of this matter, in comparison with their attitude with_ the position they took ten years .ago in this House and in this country when the project of building a second transcontinental railway m Canada was first placed before the Canadian people. We did not have then the delightful platitudes which my hon. friend the Minister of Finance and the right hon. Prime Minister gave us this afternoon about this great and glorious country and the desirability of transportation facilities being provided at the earliest possible date. I acquit the Minister of Finance of having entertained any peculiar theories ten years ago; he was walking in a different path then, and thinking on different lines, and per-hajps we may say he was a believer in some of the theories which he reiterated to-day. But the right hon. gentleman who now leads the House, kept the House sitting in the longest session since Confederation, previous to this one, in asserting the view that if Canada was to spend any money for the purpose of aiding the construction of a transcontinental railway, Canada should own the line, and he argued in 'favour of government ownership and operation. His press throughout the country declared in 1904, when my right hon. friend 'the leader of the Opposition came before the people of Canada upon this question, that the construction of a transcontinental railway was entirely unnecessary; that it would be a mortgage of the future of the Canadian people, and an expenditure wholly unjustifiable. That was the attitude of my right hon. friend ten years ago in regard to transcontinental lines.
