I took the position, on
the second reading of the Bill, I think it was, that inasmuch as the country undertook to make financial provision for the greater part of the line, it would have been more in the interests of the people to make the entire financial provision and to own the road from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

That is simply a restatement of what I said a moment ago, and a reiteration of the position my hon. friend took at that time.
Mr. GERMAIN.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend said that I opposed the construction of a .second transcontinental railroad.

If my right hon.
friend did not declare that a second transcontinental railway should not be built in 1904, I do not know what the gentlemen who went about the country looking for support as his -followers were saying to the people if they did not say that. In the province from which I come, the gentleman who contested my constituency with me, one of the prominent leaders of the Conservative party in the province of Nova Scotia, said that this tremendous burden that was to be placed on the Canadian people was wholly unnecessary and unjustifiable. So it was urged all over Canada, and in this House. If hon. gentlemen refer to 'Hansard' of 1903, they will find assertions made time after time by hon. gentlemen who calculated the amount of the mortgages that were to be placed upon the different constituencies in the Province of Ontario in securing the construction of a railway which was wholly unnecessary. I merely mention this fact for the purpose of showing more particularly that the tone of my right hon. friend has changed somewhat in the intervening years. We are delighted to know that to-day he and his party recognize the wisdom of the Liberal party and its leader in 1903, and that they believe that at that time Canada needed a second transcontinental railway, and could not have it too soon. But my right hon. friend, while urging at that time that there should be public ownership, urged a great many other things which he has not urged today in coming before the House with this proposition. What about conditions being placed in contracts providing that all freight should be carried through Canadian ports? I recall the discussion that took place in parliament at that time, during the course of which it was urged that if the Canadian people were subsidizing by subventions of various kinds the construction of a second transcontinental railway, one of the great desiderata in connection with that should be that the freight which was to go out, more particularly over these transcontinental lines, should he routed through Canadian ports. If hon. gentlemen refer to the transcontinental contracts, they will find a provision to this effect, placed there as a result of the discussion which took place in the House at that time. What about the conditions to be placed in contracts that the company which was receiving the aid should be bound to purchase in Canada the materials necessary for the construction and operation of the road? At that time this was regarded as most essential, and those hon. gentlemen who refer to ' Hansard ' of 1903 will observe the

exhaustive energy with which my right hon. friend at that time sought to devise restrictions and impose various limitations upon the company of that day, which restrictions and limitations he declared to be absolutely necessary and in the interests of the Canadian people. To-day we are asked to vote $15,000,000 without any restrictions whatever. We are asked to buy 7,000 shares of Canadian Northern stock, paying 228 for it, and to be very much pleased that we have the opportunity of doing so. That is the proposal which my right hon. friend has brought before the House, and I am bound to say that he has done so with becoming modesty. Let us see where we are in regard to this matter. The argument that we are assisting a great national enterprise is a sound argument in the abstract. I notice that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance is very apt in dealing with abstract propositions. To say that the Canadian people should to-day and at all times stand for principles of transportation improvement or anything which makes for the development and certain attainment of our future needs by these national enterprises is a proposal to which no gentleman in this House will take exception. But that does not prove my hon. friend's case. If there is any one member of this Government or of this House who should not deal with these abstract theories, and who should look after the dollars and cents and the business end of the matter, it is my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. It is open to other hon. gentlemen of the Ministry sitting around him to descant upon these glories, but I want to submit to him that he is the keeper of the keys; he is the man who is supposed to sit upon the treasury box of this Dominion, and if he does not look after the business end of this matter, who in this Government or in this House is going to do so? Theoretically, this is a national enterprise; substantially it is not a national enterprise, and for this reason.	There is a grave and
very decided line which marks off one end 'of this railway from the rest of it. The Government of the province of British Columbia has declared that the Government of the Dominion shall have nothing to do with that portion of the line which runs through British Columbia. They say: We are going to control the rates; we are going to have absolute control over everything; and the Dominion Government cannot touch this road through its Railway Commission or in any other way.
The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) pointed out very aptly and with great force, with a force that I am sure has not been met by the Prime Minister in dealing with this question, that there is a
very grave gap in connection with this proposition, great as it is, laudable as it may be, and that this Government has never attempted to deal with it at all in making this proposition and submitting it to the House. It is therefore, as a matter of fact, in a business sense, not a national proposition in any way, it is a provincial proposition in one of the greatest provinces of this Dominion. That province with its peculiar local interests and the views and judgments of its Government in respect to particular parts of this Dominion, must control this enterprise whenever it reaches its borders, to the exclusion of the interests of the rest of the Dominion, no matter how great they may be. I hope the Minister of Finance will not begin to do business in this most slovenly way. We are told by the Minister of Railways-but perhaps this is the particular function of the Minister of Railways-that there is not an atom of correspondence or a single document on file in the department in regard to this matter. That is a new way /to do business. Does the Government propose to hand out $15,000,000, no matter what reason may be urged verbally for it, to any worthy gentleman who happens to come along and see the minister and say:	I need $15,000,000
for a great national enterprise and I would be very much obliged if you would give it to me? The Minister of Finance and the Minister of Railways do not, as all responsible ministers have been accustomed to do in the past when companies and individuals approached them in regard to important matters, say to them, wiLl you be good enough to put your request in writing, state the reasons why you require this money, the position in which you are financially, the aim which you hope to obtain, the conditions under which you think the money should be granted and all other information that ought to be contained in any document presented to any minister who is going to deal with matters in a responsible . way. What would the right hon. Prime' Minister have said in 1903 if the present leader of the Opposition had then come to Parliament to deal with the proposal to construct a transcontinental railway and said: We have not a line or a letter of a document of any kind whatever in the archives of the Government to show what this proposition is? What would the leader of the Government have said if that condition of affairs had then existed? T say that such a position has never been taken in any previous period of our history. That being so here we have certain very important preliminaries which hon. gentlemen have entirely left out when they came to Parliament to deal with this question. We are told that this is a great national enterprise, that Canada wants to see it

finished, therefore give them $16,000,000. That is the position of hon. gentlemen opposite. No more argument, no more information except what can be found in the blue books and when w'e suggest that it might be wise, in the interest of the Canadian people, to give this as a loan, hon. gentlemen say: Oh no, it will not do to make this a loan because we gave more than this to theCanadianPacifiorailwayand the Grand Trunk. What kind of an answer is that? I listened in vain for the Minister of Finance to grapple with the proposition put to him by my honoured leader and to tell the committee why he did not deal with this proposition on the basis of a loan, but he has not told us, nor has the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister dealt with the question in a most gingerly fashion when he said that we must remember, take into consideration the fact that the land grants which this enterprise had received had not been made to it directly they ought not to be taken into account. My right hon. friend is too astute a gentleman in dealing with a proposition, either legal or parliamentary, not to know that it does not make any difference to the Canadian people in regard to the consideration of this question whether they got it directly or indirectly, the question is whether land which was the property of the Canadian people went to this enterprise for the purpose of ensuring the construction of a railway which went into this general proposition. If it did what is the use of my hon. friend quibbling by talking about the land going to them directly or indirectly? Then, when it was urged that in assisting the Canadian Northern you should assist it by way of a loan, my right hon. friend argued, as did the Minister of Finance, that the Grand Trunk had received more than the Canadian Northern. What has that to do with the proposition that a loan should be made, what possible relevancy has it to the suggestion that in giving aid to the Canadian Northern railway to-day we should give it by way of a loan? The result is that neither the Minister of Finance nor the Prime Minister has dealt with the proposition or suggestion made by the right hon. leader of the Opposition that it would be better to deal with this question in the way of assistance by making a loan along certain lines.
There is another phase of the question. In the absence of any correspondence or data of any kind furnished by the Canadian Northern railway, without any information being given to the House to enable us to ascertain whether or not $15,000,000 is sufficient to really aid this enterprise, we are asked to blindly vote this amount. Is the right hon. gentleman in a position to say to this House and to the country that if we vote this $15,000,000 to the Canadian Northern railway that amount will secure what we are all anxious to secure, namely, the con- I Mr. MACDONALD
struction of a third transcontinental line? Has my right hon. friend ever sought this information, is he in a position to say to this committee to-night that the Canadian Northern railway will not be back here next year asking a loan to enable them to fully complete their enterprise? Why should we not have that information? If Canada's credit is pledged to the completion of a magnificent transportation system which will involve a third transcontinental line in this country, the Government must be in a position to say, when they come to Parliament whether or not the aid which they are asking is sufficient aid, they ought to be able to tell us that it will attain the end that we all desire. The Government have taken no precautions of this kind. Either they know in regard to this question or they do not know. If they do know, they have not told the committee; if they do not know they are to be condemned because I submit that the most ordinary man, let alone a representative and trustee of the people presiding over a department or a government, would have said to parties approaching him under the conditions under which the Canadian Northern people approached the Government in regard to this matter: We require a full and a complete statement of your-affairs, we have a right to know what assistance would have to be given to you in -orderto ensure the completion of your project. The Government are in this position, they are asking the House and the country to vote $15,000,000, but whether it will produce anything, or result in the completion of this railway, they do not know, and they are leaving it to the people of the country to suppose anything they like in regard to it. Now there is some information in regard to this matter that I would like the Minister of Railways to give us. I am free to say that I do not understand the principle in this very anomalous proposal under which you are going to make a grant to the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company for their line of railway 910 miles, and another grant to the Canadian Northern Alberta Railway Company, for 260 miles of railway, two separate and distinct companies, while you propose to take from a third company, legally and in every other sense existing apart, and absolutely unconnected with two companies receiving the grant, the $7,000,000 of stock. You are giving the Canadian Northern Ontario Company and the Canadian Northern Alberta Company $16,000,000. They are not giving you anything for it, but the Canadian Northern Railway Company are going to . give you $7,000,000. We pay $16,000,000 at 228 per share, and you are handing over $16,000,000 to two different companies at the instance of the Canadian Northern Railway. Here is the situation in regard to the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Com-

pany. I find in tiie blue-book relating to railway statistics, that the total capital of the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway Company is $250,000. That is the amount of stock that has been issued, and the funded debt of that railway amounts to $12,311,000, which means that on an issued capital of one quarter of a million, the Canadian Northern Ontario Company have issued bonds or debentures to the amount of $12,300,000. The capitalization of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, which is called the parent company, is said to be $70,000,000. No information whatever is to be had in this blue-book of railway statistics, to show whether or not the Canadian Northern Alberta Company has any status whatever. We have, therefore, no source to which we can go to ascertain what their capital is, or what their present debt is, or what their financial position generally is. I endeavoured to get from the Minister of Finance this afternoon some information upon that point, but he did not have it, just as he did not have the statement, which he ought to have had, and which the Minister of Railways may be able to give us, showing how much actual cash in the way of subsidies has been granted to the Canadian Northern Railway Company in the past in connection with the construction of their enterprises. The Minister of Finance was so anxious to elaborate the technical argument he was making, as to what rights accrued, and as to what the necessities were for the construction of the transcontinental line, that he declined to give us any information in regard to that matter. The result is that while we know that the Canadian Northern Railway Company is the parent company, and while it is apparent that you are going to give money to the Canadian Northern Ontario Company and to the Canadian Northern Alberta Company, and that you are going to get stock from the Canadian Northern Railway Company- that is one thing, but when we want to find out what subsidies were given to these different companies, what actual amount of subventions have been received by them out of the treasury, we are told that it is of no consequence, and that the only thing we have to consider is the question of what was given to aid the construction of the transcontinental line.
It is in the blue-book.
Will my hon. friend be good enough to show me any information here as to the Canadian Northern Alberta Company.
No, because it did not get any subsidy, that is the reason why it is hot there.
My hon. friend seems to know more than the Minister of Railways, or the Minister of Finance. Perhaps he can give us the information as to what they did receive.
As far as I can make out from this blue book, they have received $9,700,000, including municipal aid. It is set forth in the bine book.
If the minister looks at the blue book he will find a list of companies there, and he will not find the Canadian Northern Alberta Company among them.
It is under construction, and is not in operation; that is the reason why it is not there.
Perhaps my hon. friend will be able to give us the information which I am suggesting he should have. Surely he has got some information outside of what is contained in this blue book.
There was no subsidy.

My hon. friends who are acting as a sort of assistant Ministers of Railways, seem to be full of information, if the ministers are not, in regard to this question. In response to a question of mine this afternoon, the Minister of Finance was unable to tell us whether the Canadian Northern Alberta Company was incorporated by the Dominion or by the province. That is just what I would like to know. The next thing I would like to have, is a categorical statement by the minister or by his assistants as to how much money in actual subsidies has been paid out to those different subsidiary enterprises, and how much money the country is already committed to by way of resolution or agreement.
I gave you that.

The minister's information on this question is certainly rather crude. I do not think the ministers have compared their notes. I find for instance, as will be found in ' Hansard,' that the Minister of Railways the other day told us that the total amount of guarantees by the Dominion Government to all the lines of the Canadian Northern Company was only $16,432,000.
My hon. friend is wrong. If he reads the question he will see that I referred to lines in operation, and that makes all the difference in the world.
Do I understand the minister to differentiate between lines operated and lines that are not ?
The question distinctly says routes in operation, and we gave the information exactly.

Then the minister wants us to believe that the Canadian Northern Kailway Company which now controls and operates 5,969 miles of railway, has received up to the present time, through guarantees from the Dominion Government to ensure construction, only $16,000,000 ?
Yes.

In regard to the merits of the question, I do not wish to discuss at length the financial side. Aid to railways is given, I take it-or should be given-in the interests of the people rather than in the interests of the railway company. Or, admitting that the aid given to the railway company is in the interests of the Tailway company, it is presumed that the intention of Parliament is that it shall be also in the interests of the people. My objection to the proposal now before the committee is that it is not, so far as I can gather, considered with due regard to the interests of the people. It is a ease of paying $15,000,000 for the benefit of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. I do not object to the paying of $15,000,000, but I want the payment to be for the benefit of the Canadian people as well as for the benefit of the railway company. I do not wish to counter any of the complimentary statements that have been made in regard to the Canadian Northern railway enterprises by the Minister of Railways, the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister. It is recognized that in a country of such vast extent as Canada questions of transportation must have first place if there is to be development of our country. And I must say that, for my part, I am willing to favourably recognize the effort of the Government to get rid of what appears to be an inconvenient surplus by aiding railway transportation rather than by dividing it up among the constituencies with a view to political effect more than to public benefit.
In regard to the merits of the Canadian Northern railway enterprise, while the construction of a third transcontinental railway, is of course flattering and gratifying to the national pride of Canadians, and while it must be of some material advantage to the people of Canada, I am going to take the liberty of pointing out

that this Canadian Northern railway, considered as a transcontinental enterprise is not exactly on the same footing as either the Canadian Pacific railway or the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. I speak of this, not with a view to belittling the company or the benefits it will bring, but so that we shall have a fair understanding of the exact condition. Everybody admits that the Canadian Pacific railway was essentially a pioneer enterprise. It will have to be admitted that in large part the Grand Trunk Pacific was as essentially a pioneer enterprise. The Canadian Northern railway, in that part of its line which lies between Winnipeg and Edmonton was a pioneer enterprise, but that part of its line from Edmonton to the Pacific coast, and that part of its line proposed by this resolution to be aided from Port Arthur to Ottawa is not a pioneer enterprise to anything like the degree that either the Canadian Pacific railway or the Grand Trunk Pacific was.

In the first place, for 300 miles west of Edmonton, the Canadian Northern has the benefit of the existing Grand -Trunk Pacific railway for the building of its road. In the second place, it does pot develop new country for that 300 miles, where the Grand Trunk Pacific has already developed it, the latter road having been built under absolutely pioneer and exceedingly difficult conditions. They were afterwards , acquired by the Canadian Northern railway, and the whole of this 4,000,000 acres were applied to the construction of the main line of the company from Winnipeg to Edmonton. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
I have already slated in the discussion in committee that I have no desire in any way to injure the Canadian Northern railway or its promoters, but on the other hand, I desire, as far as I can, to aid this great and useful enterprise. I think that Canada can stand three transcontinental railroads. I always thought the Canadian Pacific railway had received from the people of Canada greater aid than it should have received. However, that _ is practically ancient history. But during their construction they came to this Government for further assistance. In the first place they received $25,000,000 as a gift and also 25,000,000 acres of land. Having financed their problem and carried on their work as far as they could, they came to the Government for a loan of $25,000,000. At that time every man connected with the Canadian Pacific railway enterprise had pledged every dollar he was possessed of. The present Lord Strathcona and Lord Mount Stephen had pledged every dollar that Donald Smith and George Stephen owned; and many have done more than that, because I am inclined to think they had the Bank of Montreal pretty well pledged at that time. If that enterprise had been a failure these men would have been absolutely bankrupt. They laid their cards on the table, and said: We have done everything we can; we have confidence in this enterprise; we believe it will be a success. We have put all our capital into it, and we ask you now to come to our assistance and lend us enough money to carry out this great national enterprise. The Government of Canada said:	We will do it with the
security that you have to offer. They gave the security, which was practically a second mortgage. Why should not the same procedure be followed in this instance? Why should these gentlemen promote a railroad, own the stock, make millions of dollars out of its construction, and have the Governor in Council and the general public pay for it? It looks to me to be too absurd to merit the consideration of sensible people. I do not believe that the people of Canada are in sympathy, with the proposition which the Government is now submitting. I am not in accord with it myself, and, I beg leave to move:
That the said resolution be not now concurred in but that it be referred again to the Committee of the Whole House, with instructions to amend it by providing for an advance out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund by way of loan to tbe Canadian Northern Railway Company of a sum not exceeding fifteen million dollars for the purpose of assisting the company in completing its yearly construction; such advance to be repayable with interest half-yearly at the rate of four per cent per annum not later than the 1st of July, 1933, the advance to be secured by debentures charged upon the Mr. COCHRANE.
undertaking, equipment and property, rights and franchises of the company, and also upon the undertaking, equipment and property, rights and franchises of the Canadian Northern Pacific Railway Company, the Canadian Northern Alberta Railway Company, the Canadian Northrn Ontario Railway Company and the Canadian Northern Quebec Railway Company, ranking next after the securities already issued and at present existing against each and all of said companies, and also be further secured by a transfer to the Minister of Finance and Receiver General of Canada in trust for His Majesty, shares in the common stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company of the par value of fifteen million dollars which said stock shall be deemed to be fully paid up nonassessable and not subject to calls and to be transferred upon the books of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and which said shares of stock shall be on the repayment by the said company of the said sum of fifteen million dollars, and all interest thereon retransferred to the said company, their successors or assigns.
I make that motion because I do not believe that the Government of Canada should be a party to any corporate organization; they should not hold stock in a company or assume the position of a shareholder. It is bad in principle, and it would work out worse in practive. It would not be a good thing for the Government of Canada to be a shareholder in the Canadian Northern Railway Company or the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. I would be a party to letting the companies have all the money they require, for which they can give security, but I will not be a party to consenting that the Government shall be a shareholder in the Canadian Northern Railway Company.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
This resolution must

Before you

This resolution, however, proposes to substitute a loan for a gift; it does not increase the charge upon the revenue, but reduces it; therefore the point of order cannot be well taken.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It implies a charge
upon the revenue; otherwise its object could not be carried out. In the first place, as I understand it, the resolution cannot be moved by a private member; in the second place it cannot be moved unless it is first recommended by the Governor General. I therefore rule the motion out of order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not attach any importance to that. I have only to say that, accordingly to my understanding of the rules, I have seen many things done in this House which, I think, were entirely out of order, and I think that this motion, no matter when made, according to my interpretation of the rules with regard to money Bills or money resolutions, would be the same last year as this year. I think it is wrong now; I think it was wrong then.

I desire to offer an amendment at this stage, and I would like to be permitted to say, with all due deference, that I hardly appreciate the theory that when the Government submits in this court of Parliament a proposition, we are to be told that no one can by any possibility suggest that any change be made in the final wording of that proposition, or that no member can move the House to agree that, the proposition submitted by Mr. GRAHAM.
the Government should have attached to it any condition, or that it be amended or abbreviated in any way. It seems to me that such a proposition involves the idea that Parliament is a place where the decrees of the Government of the day are simply registered. If, through the various stages of a money Bill, from the first to the third reading, no amendment could be submitted, and if hon. gentlemen may engage in the discussion of such a Bill, but cannot ask the House to come to any conclusion different from that of the Government, the whole thing is a farce.

because the committee can always reject.

My right hon.
friend suggests that the course is open to the committee of absolutely rejecting any proposal that may be made. That does not seem to me to be at all consonant with the theory which applies to parliamentary government. If Parliament is not to be able to review any measure submitted to it, if the final statute does not mean that it is the concentrated judgment of the representatives of the people who meet here, then of course, parliamentary government is a farce. The Government of the day could introduce a money Bill, and while Parliament might agree with the principle of that Bill, it might feel that there should be something incorporated in that measure. I offer that amendment with the view of encouraging trade between East and [DOT]V;s\

in this country. That proposition is one which, 1 understand, was specially dear to the hearts of hon. gentlemen opposite, and I assume that my right hon. friend who leads the House will be disposed to accept it. If when one of the important transcontinental lines in this country comes to the Parliament of Canada and asks for special and unusual consideration, and we undertake to provide out of the public treasury of this country the immense sum of money which is now being given to them, and we say to them that we shall provide as a condition of that gift such reasonable measures as will ensure some preference at least to the trade of the eastern part of Canada going to the West, it seems to me that, unless that proposition can be adopted in this House, and that condition affixed to this gift which we are now asked to make, the position is most unique.
